events.title: Exhibit | Centering Philippine and Filipinx American Histories: Selections from The Bancroft Library
events.description: The Bancroft Library's collections of materials relating to the Philippines span nearly 500 years. Highlights in this exhibit include a transcript of an Inquisitorial trial from 1646, a prayer book written in the Cebuano language, and UC Berkeley Filipino student publications from 1905 to the present. The exhibit also features selections from the personal papers of acclaimed author Jessica Hagedorn, including typewritten drafts of her novels, poetry, song lyrics, and a screenplay, as well as childhood drawings and writings.Bancroft's renowned Latin American collections offer up intriguing examples of documents produced by the Spanish Empire as it exploited the islands' natural, cultural, and human resources. Examples include the transcript of the Inquisitorial trial of two women accused of being spiritual mediums, a manuscript written in the Jawi script, which is based on Arabic script promising religious freedom to the Muslim residents of the island of Mindanao, and materials regarding the trade between Manila and Mexico.The personal papers and published works of UC Berkeley professors Bernard Moses (1846-1931) and David Barrows (1873-1954) document their early involvement with American colonialism in the Philippines, especially their work in redesigning the Filipino education system. In the aftermath of a brutal war, Americans viewed education as a tool for pacifying a conquered population. Documentation of these professors' white supremacist views is contrasted with the work of Filipinx and Asian American scholars who use their words to critique colonialism and its racist underpinnings.Educational opportunities have brought students from the Philippines, and later Filipinx American students, to Berkeley since the early 20th century. The exhibit includes examples of four student publications — two published in the first two decades of the 1900s and two more contemporary examples — that provide evidence of these students' political engagement and their determination to make their voices heard.Selections from the personal papers of acclaimed author and performance artist Jessica Hagedorn are also on display, including examples of her novels, plays, poetry, song lyrics, a screenplay, childhood drawings, and writings. Hagedorn employs a kaleidoscope of pop culture references, songs, images, and quotes from historical figures, and a galaxy of characters representing various cultures, classes, genders, races, and nationalities in her depictions of the Philippines and Filipinx America.Open hours may vary. Please view the The Bancroft Library hours (https://www.lib.berkeley.edu/visit/bancroft) page for the most up-to-date information.

events.description: In 1985, UC Berkeley students, with support from faculty, staff, and labor unions, transformed the campus into the heart of a powerful anti-apartheid divestment campaign. They organized rallies, teach-ins, and shantytown encampments to protest the university's financial ties to companies profiting from South Africa's system of racial segregation. Divestment Now! Student Activism and the Anti-Apartheid Movement at UC Berkeley highlights a movement that mobilized thousands, politicized a new generation, and laid the groundwork for ongoing struggles for racial and economic justice.

events.title: Building Equity into Home Electrification Programs: Promises and Pitfalls in Implementation
events.description: Meeting California's ambitious greenhouse gas reduction goals requires decarbonizing its existing housing stock—replacing gas furnaces, water heaters, and stoves with electric equipment such as heat pumps, alongside improvements to insulation, wiring, and addressing health and safety problems in the home. A growing number of state and local policies and programs seek to get there, including zero-emission appliance standards and retrofit incentives, such as rebates. However, low-income households and communities of color face significant barriers to implementation, including high upfront costs, limited technical capacity, owner-renter split incentives, and displacement risk. Overcoming these barriers will not only advance the state's emissions goals but also ensure that all Californians benefit from the clean energy transition. In this webinar, we will share findings from Equitable Housing Decarbonization: Implementation Approaches, a recent study completed for the California Air Resources Board. The study draws on interviews with policymakers, energy utilities, program implementers, community organizations, and households across the state, as well as new survey-based evidence on how retrofits affect energy insecurity and well-being among low-income households. After the research presentation, panelists will discuss implementation approaches for housing decarbonization that expand access and build local communities' capacity.Please register for the webinar link. This report and webinar have been made possible by the California Air Resources Board. We are also grateful to Wells Fargo and Sobrato Philanthropies for supporting the Center's work on climate and housing solutions.

events.title: Applied Mathematics Seminar: Machine Learning for PDEs: Global Convergence and Applications to Fluid Mechanics
events.description: Speaker: Justin Sirignano, University of OxfordPhysics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) and the Deep Galerkin Method (DGM) have become widely used for physics-constrained learning and solving PDEs. In particular, DGM can solve high-dimensional (including infinite-dimensional) PDEs that are computationally intractable for traditional numerical methods. Due to the non-convexity of the PDE residual objective function used in these methods, the trained neural network may, in principle, converge to a local minimizer that does not correspond to a solution of the PDE. Consequently, there is a longstanding question regarding the mathematical foundations of these algorithms. For a class of semilinear PDEs, we prove that neural networks trained with gradient descent will converge to the PDE solution as the network width and training time become large. In the final part of the presentation, applications of machine learning to modeling turbulent flows in fluid mechanics will be discussed. A physics-based machine learning closure model is developed for the Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) equations, which outperforms existing AI for Science methods (e.g., deep operator networks, PINNs, and TBNNs) on several canonical turbulent flow cases.

events.title: Bioengineering Seminar: Noninvasive Control of Neurons Using Sonogenetics
events.description: Abstract: One approach to understanding brain function is to identify and manipulate specific neuronal circuits. While light-, and small-molecule gated approaches have been important tools for performing these manipulations, they require invasive surgical procedures or lack temporal resolution. In contrast, ultrasound-gated methods are noninvasive and have millisecond temporal precision. We identified exogenous mechanosensitive channels to sensitize target cells to noninvasive ultrasound stimuli. We termed this approach "Sonogenetics" and demonstrated its use in the nematode C. elegans. We then extended this method to the rodent model and showed that hsTRPA1 can sensitize mouse neurons to ultrasound noninvasively. Specifically, we showed that ultrasound can depolarize a neuron expressing this exogenous protein on a millisecond timescale. Furthermore, we proposed a biophysical model that provides a consistent explanation for ultrasound effects on cells. These discoveries spurred the growth of a new field, with multiple labs identifying candidate channels that function in a similar fashion. Many of these channels (TRPV1, TRPV4, TRPP2, TRPC1, TRPM4, Prestin, Piezo, TREK, TRAAK, and MscL) are mechanosensitive and have been confirmed effective in manipulating neurons in vitro and/or in vivo. Others and we have now extended this approach to cardiac muscle and non-human primates confirming the broad utility of this method. I will discuss these results and present an overview of the next steps for my group.

events.title: CTML Seminar Series: Anna Menacher (Novo Nordisk)
events.description: Join us on September 2nd to kick off our Fall 2026 CTML Seminar Series! Anna Menacher (https://www.linkedin.com/in/annamenacher/), Lead Scientist at Novo Nordisk, will start our series with her talk "Causal Inference in Pharma: Open Problems and Opportunities" This talk will take place at 12:00PM at Berkeley Way West, 5th Floor, Room 5401. Abstract: Causal inference plays an increasingly important role across pharmaceutical research, but many practically important questions remain methodologically challenging. In this talk, I will share a collection of themes and open problems that we are currently thinking about in the pharmaceutical setting. Rather than presenting a single piece of work, the aim is to give a flavour of the kinds of causal inference questions that arise in practice, highlight areas where further methodological development could be valuable, and spark discussion. I especially hope to connect with people whose research is adjacent to these problems—or who simply find them interesting—and encourage conversations and potential collaborations. Bio: Anna Menacher is a Lead Scientist at Novo Nordisk, where she works on university collaborations aimed at advancing methodological research in causal inference for the pharmaceutical industry. She received her PhD from the University of Oxford, where her research focused on Bayesian statistics and applications in neuroimaging. Her current methodological interests include longitudinal targeted maximum likelihood estimation (LTMLE), longitudinal realistic policy interventions, and target trial emulation.

events.title: Emile Chabal (University of Edinburgh) — Eric Hobsbawm: A Life
events.description: Join us as we discuss Emile Chabal's new intellectual biography of one of the foremost European intellectuals of the twentieth century: Eric Hobsbawm. In his book, Chabal offers the first substantial interpretation of Hobsbawm's entire body of writing, and explores Hobsbawm's place in — and relationship to — a remarkable network of Marxist and non-Marxist intellectuals, politicians and journalists. From jazz to peasants, Chabal traces the origins of Hobsbawm's ideas by exploring his scholarly foundations, delving deep into the archives to uncover hidden links and unexpected conversations that shaped his pathbreaking work.Emile Chabal is Professor of Contemporary History at the University of Edinburgh. He is a specialist of contemporary European political and intellectual life, with a particular interest in France.

events.title: PMB Seminar with Kent L Hill | More than an Oar: Structure and Function of the Cilium in African Trypanosomes
events.description: African trypanosomes (Trypanosoma brucei and related species) are vector-borne, protozoan parasites that cause sleeping sickness in humans and related diseases in agriculturally important livestock. Infection by these deadly pathogens causes substantial human suffering and limits economic development in some of the world's most impoverished regions. Studies from our group and others demonstrate trypanosome transmission and pathogenesis are dependent upon the parasite's single flagellum (aka cilium), a microtubule-based organelle that drives parasite motility, directs cell morphogenesis, and presents a critical platform for host-parasite interactions. The Trypanosoma genus was named for the parasite's unique, helical flagellar waveform that propagates tip to base, causing the entire cell to rotate around its long axis as it translocates with the flagellum tip leading. The parasite also engages in social motility (SoMo), using its flagellum as both sensing platform and motility machine to direct parasite navigation through tissues of the insect vector. Despite the flagellum's central importance to parasite transmission and pathogenesis, its underlying structure has previously been described in only limited detail. We have used cryo-electron microscopy to define flagellum architecture and to determine the atomic (2.8 Å)-resolution structure of flagellar doublet microtubules that are the foundation for flagellum beating and assembly. We determined the identity, structure, location, and interaction partners for 154 flagellar proteins in situ, revealing features foundational to eukaryotic flagella, while also uncovering 40 proteins found only in the pathogen and not the host, and thus present candidate drug targets. Our findings provide an atomic-scale blueprint for one of the most iconic and important structures of the trypanosome cell and expand our fundamental understanding of what it takes to build and operate a motile flagellum.

events.title: Steven Piantadosi: One idea the science of intelligent systems needs
events.description: The dual quests – to understand intelligence as it arises in biology and to build it in machines of our own making – have been with us for nearly a century. While neuroscience and psychology seek to characterize intelligence in terms of underlying neural mechanisms and emergent behavior, we still lack a set of principles that can account for how the interactions of many neurons within a brain gives rise to intelligent behavior. Meanwhile, modern AI is following a largely empirical path to create a new technology without scientific foundation. While the resulting algorithms exhibit intriguing behavior, the working principles are unknown, usage risks are incalculable, and the path to further development is unclear. The premise of this seminar is that the current century will see the emergence of a new scientific discipline – the Science of Intelligence – that seeks to elucidate universal principles that govern intelligent systems, be they biological or machine, and that this will provide both much needed insight in neuroscience and a solid foundation for technological development. The seminar will meet weekly, featuring speakers from across campus and elsewhere, who will share their views on the open questions, topics of study and debate, and relevant disciplines that a science of intelligence will encompass. Wednesday, September 2, 2026 Time: 12:00 pm Location: 101 Weill Hall Speaker: Steven Piantadosi (https://colala.berkeley.edu/people/piantadosi/) Affiliation: UC Berkeley

events.title: Alex Tamkin | How People Use AI, and What It Does to Learning and Judgment
events.location: Berkeley Way West (2121 Berkeley Way), Room 1102
events.description: Institute of Personality and Social Research ColloquiumAlex Tamkin, Member of Technical Staff, AnthropicHow People Use AI, and What It Does to Learning and Judgment AI systems are now used by millions of people daily, but we know surprisingly little about how they are actually used or what effect they have on the people using them. I present three lines of work. First, Clio, a privacy-preserving platform for studying patterns across millions of real AI conversations, and what it reveals about how people use AI for work and learning. Second, a randomized controlled trial with professional software engineers showing that AI assistance can impair skill formation, but that how people interact with AI matters as much as whether they use it: people who asked for explanations learned more than those who delegated their work. Third, ongoing work on how experts make judgment calls when working alongside AI agents, and what this means for human oversight. I will close with open questions about how people can preserve their own agency as they rely on AI for more of their thinking and work, and would welcome the group's input. Alex Tamkin is a researcher at Anthropic. His work spans AI safety and societal impacts, including how AI is used in the world and what it means for work, learning, and the distribution of power. He previously led research on the Anthropic Economic Index and Clio, a privacy-preserving platform for understanding real-world AI usage.If you require an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact Ore Carmi [Tel: 510-642-5050; Email: orecarmi@berkeley.edu] with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days in advance of the event.

events.title: Spectral Theory Seminar: Entanglement and circuit complexity in random linear optical networks
events.description: Speaker: Laura Shou, University of MarylandWe study the growth of entanglement and circuit complexity in random linear optical networks as a function of the circuit depth. For entanglement dynamics, we start with an initial Gaussian state with all n modes equally squeezed. For random brickwall circuits, we show that entanglement, as measured by the Rényi-2 entropy, grows diffusively as a function of the depth, in contrast to the linear growth for random qubit brickwall circuits. We also consider robust circuit complexity for random 1D brickwall circuits, and show that it scales at most diffusively in the depth with high probability, again in contrast to the linear scaling for certain random qubit circuits. Joint work with Joseph Iosue, Yu-Xin Wang, Victor Galitski, and Alexey Gorshkov.

events.title: James Nuñez: Rewriting the human epigenome
events.description: The epigenome is essential to regulate gene expression in human cells and undergoes dynamic changes during embryogenesis, aging, and in disease. I will present our efforts to dissect how the epigenome is remodeled and established de novo, focusing on DNA methylation - the most abundant epigenetic modification on the human genome. By blending our CRISPR-based tools for epigenome editing with genome-wide genetic screens and proximity-dependent proteomics, we discover an unexpected interplay between RNA m6A modifications and de novo DNA methylation to program heritable epigenetic silencing of transposable elements. Additionally, I will highlight our work to expand the available tools for locus-specific epigenome editing that have broad use for studying epigenetic pathways, functional genomics, synthetic biology, and as potential therapeutic medicines.Division(s): Divisions of Biochemistry, Biophysics & Structural Biology, Division of Cell Biology, Development & Physiology, and Genetics, Genomics, Evolution & Development

events.title: Probability Seminar: Jiaoyang Huang "Random matrix statistics and loop equations"
events.description: Abstract: Universality in random matrix theory states that, after appropriate rescaling, local eigenvalue statistics in the bulk converge to the Sine point process, while those at the spectral edge converge to the Airy point process. In particular, the extreme eigenvalues exhibit Tracy–Widom fluctuations. In this talk, I will present direct characterizations of these universal statistics through loop equations. The resulting uniqueness theorems provide a new route to proving universality: it suffices to verify the corresponding approximate loop equations for the ensemble under consideration. This is joint work with Paul Bourgade.

events.title: EECS Colloquium | Beyond Brute Force: The Era of Adaptive Intelligence
events.description: The next generation of truly intelligent systems won't be defined by scale. They'll be defined by adaption: the ability to continuously learn, evolve, and close the gap between what a model knows and what the world actually looks like right now. In this talk, Sara Hooker, Co-founder of Adaption, defines the paradigm shift of moving beyond monolithic, static AI and what it takes to build systems that are malleable by design. She'll cover the principles behind continual, gradient-free learning, and why the next era of intelligence evolves with the world. Her goal is to build AI that works for people, not the other way around. Sara Hooker is a co-founder of Adaption Labs, which builds intelligence that continuously evolves. Sara leads a large team of AI researchers and engineers that build extremely efficient, adaptable systems. Sara Hooker was previously VP of Research at Cohere, and prior to Cohere, she built large systems in computer vision and NLP at Google DeepMind. Her research has been published in top venues including Nature, NeurIPS, ICML, ACL, ICLR, EMNLP, MLSys, and has been recognized with honors such as the ACL Best Paper Award and CACM front cover for her work on the Hardware Lottery. Her work has been featured in mainstream news outlets including TechCrunch, The New York Times, The Washington Post, Axios, MIT Technology, and The Atlantic.

events.title: ERG Colloquium Series Fall 2026: Johann Frick
events.description: This talk will be an introduction to population ethics, the branch of philosophy that investigates ethical issues surrounding the creation of new people. The power we wield over the future is immense: our choices today not only shape the quality of future lives but often determine who will exist in the first place. What does it mean to act ethically toward individuals whose very existence hinges on our decisions? We will explore this question by reflecting on cases that range from personal choices about procreation to sweeping societal actions like climate change policy. Along the way, we will confront the Non-Identity Problem—a deep philosophical puzzle that challenges our intuitions about harm, responsibility, and what it means to do the right thing for future generations. (B.Phil., Oxford; Ph.D., Harvard). His main interests span moral and political philosophy, practical reason, and applied ethics. His current work focuses on population ethics, the ethics of risk, moral dilemmas and moral luck, the notion of interpersonal justification, and the ethics of immigration and national partiality. Publications include "Contractualism and Social Risk" (Phil. & Public Affairs, 2015), "What We Owe to Hypocrites" (Phil. & Public Affairs, 2016), "National Partiality, Immigration, and the Problem of Double-Jeopardy" (Oxford Studies in Political Phil. 2020) and "Conditional Reasons and the Procreation Asymmetry" (Philosophical Perspectives, 2020).

events.title: Free Exercise's False Binary: Lessons from Jewish Law
events.description: This lecture puts Jewish law in conversation with the ongoing debate over how the Free Exercise Clause of the First Amendment should be construed. A bedrock assumption in free exercise jurisprudence is that religion's mandates are absolute. But religious norms do not always operate that way. Jewish law, for example, is often nonbinary and spectrum-based. It is an elaborate system of flexible standards and sliding-scale rules that enables religious practitioners to live under secular rule. Jewish law, then, allows us to reexamine a common assumption underlying free exercise jurisprudence. It also raises the question whether, in some instances at least, religious freedom itself incentivizes the reshaping of religion as unyielding where previously it was understood to be flexible.To register for this event, please click this link.ZalmanRothschild is an Assistant Professor of Law and the Horn Family Distinguished Research Scholar in Law and Religion at the Benjamin N. Cardozo School of Law. He holds a J.D., magna cum laude, from Harvard Law School and a Ph.D. from New York University. His scholarship has appeared in the Columbia Law Review, Cornell Law Review, Georgetown Law Journal, Harvard Law Review Forum, and Yale Law Journal Forum, and has been featured in The New York Times, The New Yorker, and The New York Review of Books. His popular writing has appeared in The New York Times, The Atlantic, The Guardian, and The Washington Post. He has testified before Congress on religion and public schools and has delivered, or is scheduled to deliver, several named lectures, including the Fishman Family Endowed Lecture at Vassar College, the Krivosha Lecture at the University of Nebraska, and the Robert M. Cover Lecture in Law and Religion at Yale Law School. The Law and Religion Section of the Association of American Law Schools has twice awarded him the Harold Berman Award for Excellence in Scholarship. events.title: Neyman Seminar with Alex Strang: Symmetry Exploiting Diagonalization Procedures for Fast Particle Detection in Cryo-EM
events.description: Symmetry Exploiting Diagonalization Procedures for Fast Particle Detection in Cryo-EM Cryogenic electron microscopy can produce extremely high precision images of cell cross-sections. To find specific target molecules, a template matching search repeatedly convolves the image against an ensemble of simulated projections of the target. Different orientations, depths, and conformations of the target produce different projections. Possible detections are selected by identifying peaks in the resulting correlograms. Standard template matching searches demand tens of millions of separate convolutions, one per hypothesized orientation, depth, and conformation, each against a high resolution image. The associated operation is equivalent to a large matrix vector product, and is prohibitively expensive, even when the spatial convolution is accelerated using the FFT. We present a multi-precision approach, which takes advantage of the fact that the vast majority of the correlations computed are far removed from the decision threshold, so need not be computed to more than their first digits. This allows a two-stage search whose first stage produces approximate correlations by replacing the large matrix operation with its low rank approximation, and whose second stage recomputes only the correlation values that demand high precision. To perform the first stage, we need to decompose the template matching matrix. Full template matching matrix are too large to decompose directly. However, the entire search process is symmetric under in-plane rotations. This induces a block circulant symmetry in the template matching matrix which can be exploited to speed decomposition. We discuss a general symmetry-exploiting SVD routine that reduces a single large SVD problem into many small SVD problems that can be solved in parallel. The routine applies to any block-circulant matrix and to any matrix that commutes with a permutation. We derive a separable form for the eigenfunctions of linear operators that exhibit the same symmetries, and relate the separable form to the theory of steerable filters and Lie groups. This theory fully generalizes the observation that linear operators that commute with translations are diagonalized by a Fourier transform to linear operators that commute with smoothly parameterized bijective transformations. We conclude by illustrating the decomposition of large template matching matrices in less time than is required to simulate the matrix entries.

events.title: Combinatorics Seminar: Electroid varieties and the Lagrangian Grassmannian
events.description: Speaker: Mia Smith, University of MichiganRecent work of Lam, Chepuri–George–Speyer, and Bychkov–Gorbounov–Kazakov–Talalaev gave a stratification of the totally nonnegative Lagrangian Grassmannian into electroid cells parameterized by cactus networks, paralleling Postnikov's stratification of the totally nonnegative Grassmannian by positroid cells. Electroid varieties arise as an algebro-geometric extension of electroid cells. In analogy to results of Knutson, Lam, and Speyer on positroid varieties, electroid varieties are reduced, irreducible, regular in codimension one, compatibly Frobenius split, and form a stratification. In this talk, I'll describe our recent work proving these geometric properties of electroid varieties and give a flavor of the combinatorics underlying some of the proofs. This talk is based on joint work with Dawei Shen and David Speyer.

events.title: "Memories in Motion: Selected Stories of Mildred Howard" Screening and Q+A
events.location: Maude Fife Room, 315 Wheeler Hall, UC Berkeley
events.description: RSVP to attend (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSdTLG9junL70omZ_RpGJEPSCzRu7SYOgVwYHKGp9H4F9p0Vag/viewform?usp=dialog). Join us for the first public screening of Memories in Motion: Selected Stories of Mildred Howard, which premiered at the Oakland Museum of California on Juneteenth. The documentary traces the spaces, moments, and relationships that have shaped the life and work of world-renowned artist Mildred Howard across eight decades rooted in the East Bay. Co-written and directed by Howard's grandson, Lamar "MYL3Z" Brown, and Delency Parham, a second-year Ph.D. student in the Department of African American and African Diaspora Studies at UC Berkeley, the film offers an intimate portrait of Howard's life, practice, and community. The screening will be followed by a conversation and Q&A featuring Mildred Howard, MYL3Z, Professor Leigh Raiford, and graduate student Irene Denise Ross. A by-product of the second great migration, in which an influx of Black Southerners headed West looking for wartime jobs, Mildred Howard (b.1945) is a cross-disciplinary artist born in San Francisco, raised in Berkeley, and currently living in Oakland, CA. The child of community organizers and self-taught creatives, her practice spans design, sculpture, and mixed-media assemblages. Mildred's artistic ethos and objectives have been to "make every piece reflective of the community where it exists, and to make people question or come up with their own interpretation of what is." From June 12, 2026–October 11, 2026, OMCA will exhibit a retrospective of Mildred's work titled, Poetics of Memory, which will feature select pieces from her 50-year career. Many call him an artist; Lamar "MYL3Z" Brown calls himself a maker. A Berkeley native, he builds meaning through mixed‑media assemblage—transforming found objects into tactile structures that map memory, place, lineage, and experience. His earliest and most formative training came from spending his entire life as an assistant artist to his grandmother Mildred Howard, learning by watching, helping, and absorbing the discipline, curiosity, and intention behind her practice. That foundation shaped his understanding of what it means to make—use what's given, honor the lineage, and push the work farther.Leigh Raiford is Professor of African American and African Diaspora Studies at the University of California, Berkeley, where she teaches, researches, curates and writes about Black visuality and world-making. At UC Berkeley, Raiford also co-directs with Tianna S. Paschel the Black Studies Collaboratory, an ongoing initiative to amplify the world-building work of Black Studies supported by funds from the Andrew W. Mellon Foundation, the Spencer Foundation and the San Francisco Foundation.Irene Denise Ross is a writer, director, and curator exploring how artists fashion a poetics of Black sociality. A recent graduate of Columbia University's MA program in African American and African Diaspora Studies (2023) and Princeton University's undergraduate program in African American Studies (2020), Irene is a doctoral student at U.C. Berkeley, with a focus in African American Studies, Film Studies, and Theater and Performance. Disciplinary engagements range from contemporary Afro-surrealism, Visual Poetics, Media Studies, Political Theory, and Black Feminist Geographies – to beloved thriller and comedy classics, and the stylings that mark each genre.

events.title: Building Equity into Home Electrification Programs: Promises and Pitfalls in Implementation
events.description: Meeting California's ambitious greenhouse gas reduction goals requires decarbonizing its existing housing stock—replacing gas furnaces, water heaters, and stoves with electric equipment such as heat pumps, alongside improvements to insulation, wiring, and addressing health and safety problems in the home. A growing number of state and local policies and programs seek to get there, including zero-emission appliance standards and retrofit incentives, such as rebates. However, low-income households and communities of color face significant barriers to implementation, including high upfront costs, limited technical capacity, owner-renter split incentives, and displacement risk. Overcoming these barriers will not only advance the state's emissions goals but also ensure that all Californians benefit from the clean energy transition. In this webinar, we will share findings from Equitable Housing Decarbonization: Implementation Approaches, a recent study completed for the California Air Resources Board. The study draws on interviews with policymakers, energy utilities, program implementers, community organizations, and households across the state, as well as new survey-based evidence on how retrofits affect energy insecurity and well-being among low-income households. After the research presentation, panelists will discuss implementation approaches for housing decarbonization that expand access and build local communities' capacity.Please register for the webinar link. This report and webinar have been made possible by the California Air Resources Board. We are also grateful to Wells Fargo and Sobrato Philanthropies for supporting the Center's work on climate and housing solutions.

events.title: Stephen Small | Transnational Black culture in Liverpool at the end of the twentieth century: anomalous legacies in the 'slaving capital of the world' aka 'the second city of Empire'
events.location: Social Science Matrix, 820 Social Sciences Building.
events.description: In the 1950s the Black population (Afro-Caribbean and African) of England was estimated at no more than 50,000; by the 1970s it had increased to 400,000 and by 2001, the census reported it was over 1.1 million. Most research on Black Britain in this period is focused on the population at the center of this increase, the so-called 'Windrush Generation' – that is, West Indian settlers that arrived since the 1940s, developed family units with two West Indian parents, primarily in London, and with limited firsthand experience or collective memory of legacies of slavery and imperialism in England itself. This research is reflected in the work of scholars like Stuart Hall, Paul Gilroy, Hazel Carby, Heidi Mirza and John Solomos. Hall highlighted how 'Black is not a question of pigmentation … [It] is a historical category, a political category, a cultural category'; and Mirza insisted that 'It is only by attention to situated localised accounts of 'marginalised lives' that we can reveal the ways of 'being and becoming' a gendered, sexed, raced and classed subject'. While Black Liverpool shared much in common with Black London and other cities in this period, Liverpool's assemblage of features - what I denote as a racialised anomaly - was markedly different. There were far more Africans than West Indians, more long-term citizens than recent immigrants, the highest proportion of inter-racial marriages and people of mixed racial origins in the nation, more extensive first-hand experiences, and a far more vivid collective memory of imperialism in West Africa. These differences arose from the city's distinctive involvement in slavery and imperialism, the settlement in imperial Liverpool of (overwhelmingly male) seamen from West Africa; and the forced concentration of Black and multi-racial families in one neighbourhood (Liverpool 8 - later known as Toxteth). The city historically also had a far greater reliance on port activities and consistently higher rates of unemployment than in any other English city. In this presentation, drawing in his recently published book – Black Liverpool: 'the real thing' - Professor Stephen Small will examine how the historical and structural features of Black Liverpool gave rise to unique configurations of Black cultural expression in that city in the final decades of the twentieth century. Specifically, how the Black community in Liverpool pursued, embraced and transformed waves of transnational Black culture from West Africa, the West Indies and the United States in the final three decades of the twentieth century. The role of gender ideologies, institutional practices and the agency and experiences of Black women are closely examined. One implication of this study is that an analysis of Black Britain based on a London-centered account of the so-called 'Windrush Generation' is unrepresentative and misleading.Stephen Small is a Professor of the Graduate School in the Department of African American and African Diaspora Studies at the University of California, Berkeley, a position he began in January 2025 after he retired from 30 years teaching on campus. He researches the history and sociology of Black people across the diaspora, with a primary focus on legacies of slavery and imperialism, public history and collective memory. He is a faculty member of the Black Europe Summer School (BESS) (since 2007) – a two-week program in Amsterdam, founded and directed for Dr. Kwame Nimako; and has held visiting positions at universities in Brazil, England, France, Japan, the Netherlands, Spain, and Zimbabwe. He was Guest Curator at the Merseyside Maritime Museum's Atlantic Slave Trade Gallery (now the International Slavery Museum) in Liverpool that opened in 1994. His most recent book is Black Liverpool: 'The real thing' West African, West Indian and Afro-American Culture at the end of the twentieth century published by Liverpool University Press in June 2026. Recent publications include In the Shadows of the Big House: Twenty-First Century Antebellum SlaveCabins and Heritage Tourism in Louisiana (2023) and 1981- Black Liverpool, Past and Present (2022) (co-written with Jimi Jagne). He is also co-editor (with Darlene Clark Hine and Trica Danielle Keaton) of Black Europe and the African Diaspora (2009). Stephen earned his Ph.D. in Sociology at the University of California, Berkeley (1989); his MS.C in Social Sciences from the University of Bristol (1983); and his B.A. (honours) in Economics and Sociology from the University of Kent at Canterbury (1979). Stephen was born and raised in Liverpool, England – the city with the nation's longest-standing Black population. events.title: Mark Plitt (Postdoc, Fisher Lab): A monoamine instructs head direction plasticity
events.description: Many plasticity rules rely on adjusting the strength of synapses between pairs of cells based on their coincident activity. We uncovered a new mechanism for coincidence detection in the Drosophila head direction network. To maintain an accurate sense of direction, head direction neurons that signal orientation during navigation must learn to anchor to relevant external sensory cues in novel environments. Yet the synaptic mechanism for this form of unsupervised learning is unknown in any organism. In Drosophila, GABAergic visual inputs converge onto head direction neurons, and these inhibitory synapses change strength with experience to learn the relationship between visual landmarks and head direction. However, how coincident pre- and postsynaptic activity is detected across this inhibitory synapse is not understood. We discovered that neurons which release the monoamine octopamine close a feedback loop that conveys postsynaptic head direction activity onto presynaptic terminals of visual inputs. This octopamine pathway is required for anchoring the head direction network to visual cues. Furthermore, pairing structured activation of octopamine neurons with a visual cue is sufficient to drive rapid plasticity, even without postsynaptic head direction cell activity. Previous work has extensively characterized coincidence detection mechanisms at excitatory synapses; our work defines a novel mechanism for coincidence detection at an inhibitory synapse, in which postsynaptic activity is relayed via a neuromodulatory neuron onto presynaptic terminals.

events.title: Berkeley Art, Law, and Finance Project: Hidden Layers: AI Infrastructures and Hallucinations Opening Reception
events.description: Co-sponsored by the Berkeley Art, Law, and Finance Project, Hidden Layers (https://german.berkeley.edu/news/upcoming-exhibitions-hidden-layers-ai-infrastructures-and-hallucinations) brings together international artists working at the intersection of contemporary art and machine learning to make visible the layers of artificial intelligence that normally stay out of sight: among them, its planetary infrastructure, its ideological biases, its unexpected outputs. Taking the "hidden layers" of neural networks as its conceptual frame, the exhibition asks what AI conceals and what it invents, foregrounding the hallucinations, biases, and latent spaces through which these systems generate images, texts, and worlds. Participating artists include Nouf Aljowaysir, Gašper Beguš, Nina Beguš & Metahaven, Grégory Chatonsky, Jill Miller & Asma Kazmi, Greg Niemeyer, Mario Santamaria & Alex Saum-Pascual, and more to be announced. events.title: Exhibition Opening Reception: "Hidden Layers: AI Infrastructures and Hallucinations"
events.location: Worth Ryder Art Gallery, Anthropology & Art Building, Rm 116
events.description: The Department of German and the Department of Art Practice are excited to announce the opening of Hidden Layers: AI Infrastructures and Hallucinations, curated by Antonio Somaini with Hannes Bajohr and Sonja Thiel, in dialogue with the France–Berkeley research initiative The Latent Spaces of Culture, and on display at the Worth Ryder Art Gallery. This exhibition examines some of the concealed dimensions of contemporary AI culture — the planetary infrastructures of extraction and computation, the often invisible human labor, the latent vector spaces within which culture is compressed and processed, and the models' hallucinations. Hidden Layers tackles these phenomena from two different perspectives: AI Infrastructures and AI Hallucinations. Featuring works by Nouf Aljowaysir; Gašper and Nina Beguš & Metahaven; Grégory Chatonsky; Kate Crawford & Vladan Joler; Asma Kazmi & Jill Miller; Andrea Khôra; Occitane Lacurie & Barnabé Sauvage; Greg Niemeyer; and Mario Santamaria & Alex Saum-Pascual. The project is a collaboration between the Department of German and the Worth Ryder Art Gallery at the Department of Art Practice.Exhibition Dates: September 3 - October 3, 2026Opening Reception: Thursday, September 3, 4-6:30pm, Worth Ryder Art Gallery RSVP here (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSd_OOMe7YQHw3CYbSr673UCSlQ0f4mn4lZ7g46KhRUTRpC5qQ/viewform?usp=dialog)Artist Talk, Gregory Chatonsky: Thursday, September 3, 6:30-8:00pm, AAPB 285 RSVP here (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSd_OOMe7YQHw3CYbSr673UCSlQ0f4mn4lZ7g46KhRUTRpC5qQ/viewform?usp=dialog)Related programming:Film Program: September 9, 7 pm, BAMPFA Workshop on Latent Spaces of Culture: September 9, 2pm-4pm; September 10/11, 9:30 am-4pm on both days, 470 Stephens Additional events and more details to be announced. Fong and Family Distinguished Chair in China Studies, the Division of Arts & Humanities, the Townsend Center for the Humanities and the School of Information, the Technology Network of the Berkeley Economy and Society Initiative (BESI); and the Berkeley Art, Law, and Finance Project, hosted by the Berkeley Center for Law and Business at Berkeley Law. events.title: Artist Talk - Grégory Chatonsky: INFRALLUCINATION
events.description: French-Canadian artist Grégory Chatonsky, a pioneer of net art and among the first artists to work through machine learning presents a lecture titled "INFRALLUCINATION."Hallucination has become the ambivalent concept of our digital era: oscillating between an error to be corrected and a driver of radical inventiveness. Far from abstract theories, this conference proposes approaching artificial hallucination through the lens of artistic experience. Gregory Chatonsky explores how AI redefines our relationship with reality and memory. Through a journey across his works, he questions: how does a machine hallucinate? How does this "ontological pareidolia" transform our own imagination? A reflection on a machine that, through its signs, becomes the language-based hallucination of the world. Free and open to the public.RSVP here (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSd_OOMe7YQHw3CYbSr673UCSlQ0f4mn4lZ7g46KhRUTRpC5qQ/viewform?usp=dialog)Related programming: Exhibition: Hidden Layers: AI Infrastructures and HallucinationsExhibition Dates: September 3 - October 3, 2026 Opening Reception: Thursday, September 3, 4-6:30pm, Worth Ryder Art GalleryArtist Talk, Gregory Chatonsky "INFRALLUCINATION": Thursday, September 3, 6:30-8:00pm, AAPB 285Film Program, Push Buttons and AI (https://bampfa.org/event/push-buttons-and-ai): September 9, 7 pm, BAMPFACuratorial Tour, led by Antonio Somaini: Friday, September 11, 4:30pm, Worth Ryder Art GalleryWorkshop on Latent Space of Culture: September 9, 2pm-4pm; September 10/11, 9:30 am-4pm on both days, 470 StephensSalon on AI and Art: September 16, 6pm– 9pm, AI Futures LabTour of AI: October 3 Reservations required. events.title: ASRB Case Workshop
events.description: The Association for Socially Responsible Business (ASRB) is recruiting! ASRB consults for companies, nonprofits, and government agencies on sustainability and social issues. Our past clients include Google, Sweetgreen, Staples, and the World Bank. On these client-facing projects, our undergraduate members build skills like public speaking and analytical thinking, often applying what they learn in the classroom. Members take on ownership of projects and move into leadership roles, and they leave with a first professional experience, exposure to a wide range of industries, and professional development resources. Alumni have gone on to leading firms in consulting, finance, energy, and technology, to nonprofits and public sector work, and to graduate school, including law school, medical school, master's and PhD programs. Beyond projects, ASRB is unique for its tight-knit community, which sustains traditions such as our big-little system, volunteering with the City of Berkeley, our semesterly retreat, and other programming that builds lasting relationships. We value diversity of ideas and welcome students from all backgrounds and majors. No prior experience is required. Come meet us: Joint Info Session: Monday, August 31st, 8–9pm, Valley Life Sciences Building 2060 ASRB Info Session: Tuesday, September 1st, 8–9:30pm, Dwinelle Hall 130 Case Interview Workshop: Thursday, September 3rd, 7–9pm, on Zoom (link at asrbatberkeley.com) Applications close Saturday, September 5th. For more information, visit asrbatberkeley.com or fill out our interest form .

events.title: Film Screening: Saint Omer
events.description: Alice Diop's first venture into narrative after more than a decade of documentary filmmaking, Saint Omer follows a young novelist, Rama (Kayije Kagame), who is observing the trial of Laurence Coly (Guslagie Malanda), a woman accused of murdering her fifteen-month-old child in northern France. Based on a real-life 2016 trial in the French town the film borrows its title from, Diop's haunting retelling is nuanced and charged with provocations about motherhood, immigration, and abandonment. "An intellectually charged, emotionally wrenching story about the inability of storytelling—literary, legal or cinematic—to do justice to the violence and strangeness of human experience" (A.O. Scott, New York Times).

events.title: Rethinking Linking: Effects of Cap-and-Trade Integration Equilibrium Emissions and Welfare | Thor Larson
events.description: Job Candidate Presentation Abstract Conventional economic reasoning suggests that linking cap-and-trade programs creates efficiency gains by lowering costs while holding emissions constant. When cap-and-trade programs have price floors or ceilings, however, linking may increase emissions and decrease welfare. I investigate this phenomenon within California and Québec, where cap-and-trade linkage increased emissions by 17.5 million tons CO2e and reduced welfare by $331 million annually – an outcome that was ex-ante foreseeable. A reformed linked market could have remained emissions-neutral while instead increasing welfare by up to $32 million annually. I argue that political and institutional frictions prevented such reforms from being implemented and propose that policy makers prioritized cutting emissions cheaply over equating marginal damages and benefits. Given these constraints, linking with trading ratios remains incentive-compatible and recovers over three-fifths of potential emissions-neutral welfare gains.

events.description: Speaker: Izhar Oppenheim, Ben Gurion UniversityHigher-rank universal lattices and Steinberg groups over Z[t1,…,tm] can be viewed as generalizations of higher-rank algebraic lattices. In this lecture, I will discuss results showing that these groups possess the fixed point property for all affine isometric actions on uniformly convex Banach spaces. This result provides a far-reaching extension of my earlier work on Banach property (T) for SL(n,Z) that was later generalized by de Laat and de la Salle for all higher rank algebraic lattices.

events.title: Film Screening: We
events.description: We takes viewers along the suburban RER B train line of Paris, which runs physically from north to south yet metaphorically ranges across the entire breadth of Parisian, French, and global humanity. The film introduces writers, nurses, cleaning ladies, garage mechanics, and more, all representing the many disparate communities that ring Paris, yet each unique enough to remind us that no one—and no one film, book, or song—could ever represent such a wide array of voices and lives. "A tender homage to the unnoticed" (The Guardian).

events.title: CNMAT Concert: Matteo Cesari & Simone Conforti
events.description: Matteo Cesari & Simone Conforti play works for flute and electronics from Kaija Saariaho, Eva Reiter, Simone Conforti, & Marco Stroppa.Matteo Cesari Flutes Simone Conforti Flute and Electronics ProgramInTheEventThatDuskMeetsDawn, Simone Conforti For two flutes, world premiere NoaNoa, Kaija Saariaho For flute and electronics Konter (transcription for contrabass flute in C - Matteo Cesari), Eva ReiterFor contrabass flute and electronics PastiCity, Simone Conforti Fixed media Little i, Marco Stroppa For flutes and chamber electronics Matteo Cesari is internationally recognised as one of the leading interpreters of contemporary flute repertoire. Recipient of the Kranichsteiner Musikpreis at Darmstadt, he has performed at venues including the Philharmonie de Paris, Elbphilharmonie Hamburg, Pierre Boulez Saal Berlin and Teatro Colón Buenos Aires. His activity combines performance, creation, artistic research and pedagogy, with long-term collaborations including Salvatore Sciarrino, Alberto Posadas, Georges Aperghis and Brian Ferneyhough. He has contributed to more than thirty premieres and participated closely in projects including the rewriting of Sciarrino's L'Opera per flauto, vol. 3. A permanent member of Ensemble Multilatérale and faculty at IRCAM / Pôle Sup'93, his recent work increasingly focuses on contrabass flute, electronics and new artistic formats linking interpretation, technology and listening. Born in Winterthur, Switzerland, Simone Conforti is a composer, Computer Music Designer, wind instrument performer, and software developer. He holds a Ph.D. in Media Studies, as well as degrees in Flute and Electronic Music Composition. He currently serves as Computer Music Designer and Professor at IRCAM in Paris. He has previously taught Electroacoustic Composition and Computer Music at the Conservatories of Cuneo and Florence, and worked as a Computer Music Designer and tutor at the CIMM of the Venice Biennale. His research activity has taken him to institutions across Europe, including the University of Basel, HEM Geneva, HEMU Lausanne, and MARTLab in Florence. Driven by a deep curiosity for emerging music technology, has founded several companies pioneering automatic music generation and algorithmic approaches to 3D sound diffusion and sound masking. His work has been published by Suvini Zerboni, Da Vinci Classics, Mode, Stradivarius, Die Schachtel, Third Man Records, Cramps, Audiomat, Mudima Music, ET'CETERA, A14, Nardini Editore, Kehrer Verlag, Dissonance, SAGE Publishing, AIB – Associazione Italiana Biblioteche, Artestampa, and Transcript.

events.title: Film Screening: Breathless
events.description: Jean-Luc Godard's films of the 1960s are rich in intellectual references, gorgeous visuals, and music by Michel Legrand—classically French, in their postmodern way. But scrappy, jazzy, black-and-white Breathlessremains what Russell Merritt called "the outlaw artifact of the nouvelle vague." A very young Jean-Paul Belmondo plays the outlaw hero Michel Poiccard (alias Laszlo Kovacs), who kills a cop and hides in plain sight in Paris. An even younger Jean Seberg announces herself loudly as an American student working for the New York Herald Tribune. "A thrilling reminder of how playful Godard could be" (Ella Taylor, Village Voice).

events.title: Film Screening: Mean Streets
events.description: Set during the Feast of San Gennaro in the Italian neighborhood where Martin Scorsese grew up, and populated with characters and situations based on the neighborhood's inhabitants, Mean Streets is an early distillation of the themes that would define the director's career. Charlie (Harvey Keitel) is torn between his devout Catholicism, his commitment to his volatile friend Johnny Boy (Robert De Niro), a romantic entanglement with Johnny's cousin Teresa, and opportunities offered by his crime boss uncle. Crackling with creative energy, this now iconic neo-noir is inflected with influences from French New Wave, cinema verité, and American independent filmmakers like Kenneth Anger, John Cassavetes, and Shirley Clarke.

events.title: Exploration of Forms: Movement as Creative Practice, a three-part workshop with Randee Paufve
events.description: About Exploration of Forms: Exploration of Forms is a public workshop series that centers embodiment, transformation, and creativity. All workshops are free for students. Guests are encouraged to make a donation of $25 at the door, but no one will be turned away for lack of funds.Signups are available here: https://tdps.link/explorationAbout This Workshop:This workshop series investigates movement not as a set of skills to acquire, but as a creative and expressive practice to inhabit and sustain. Drawing on modern/contemporary and jazz dance techniques and performance practices, each session builds on the last — offering dancers a framework for thinking about their relationship to technique, expression, and the long arc of a life in movement.September 6th - Session 1:Technique as a Tool for Expression - What is technique for? This session uses rigorous contemporary movement — warmup, floor progressions, combinations — as a lens for examining how technical training shapes (and can liberate) individual expression. Dancers are invited to bring their bodies and their questions. September 13th - Session 2:Performance Presence and the Moving Body - How does a dancer inhabit a moment rather than execute it? This session explores performance technique not as a set of presentational skills but as a practice of attention — to space, to music, to other bodies, and to the intelligence moving through your own. September 20th - Session 3: Sustaining a Creative Practice - What keeps us dancing? This session addresses the longer questions beneath the work: how dancers build and maintain a creative practice over time, how they stay curious, how they metabolize influences, and how they find their own movement voice. Includes movement work alongside structured reflection. About the Teacher: Randee Paufve is a choreographer, dancer, teacher, and Artistic Director of Paufve Dance. A 2019 Fulbright Scholar and recipient of the Isadora Duncan Dance Award for Outstanding Individual Performance, she has been featured on NPR's All Things Considered and honored with the inaugural Della Davidson Prize for Innovations in Dance-Theater. Her work has been presented nationally at ODC Theater, SFMOMA, the Mondavi Center, On the Boards, and the Portland Institute for Contemporary Art, and internationally in India, Austria, and Portugal. She has taught on the faculties of UC Davis, CSU Sacramento, St. Mary's College of California, University of San Francisco and Lewis and Clark College, and Shawl-Anderson Dance Center. Accessibility: If you require an accommodation for effective communication or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact us with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7–10 days in advance of the event.

events.title: Film Screening: A Woman is a Woman
events.description: Jean-Luc Godard's third feature was conceived "within the framework of a neorealist musical," with nods to René Clair and Ernst Lubitsch. Anna Karina is Angela, an occasional stripper in a shabby club called the Zodiac. She is determined to have a baby and soon; when her lover Emile (Jean-Claude Brialy) won't, she turns to his friend Alfred Lubitsch (Jean-Paul Belmondo), who will. There is magic in this film, from actual hat tricks to the famous egg-frying gag to the mesmerizing traveling shots. Godard's sense of woman as mystery is a part of that magic. (Even the title throws up its hands.)

events.title: Empowered by AI: Create a More Breathable, Sustainable Workday (2026 Fall NOW Encore Series)
events.description: 2026 NOW Encore Series (https://hr.berkeley.edu/development/career-development/workshops) Higher education staff are navigating unprecedented workload pressures: increasing demands, shrinking resources, and the nonstop expectation to do more with less. Meanwhile, AI has entered the workplace—but most employees are unsure how to use it effectively, ethically, or in ways that genuinely reduce overwhelm rather than add to it. This session reframes AI through a human-centered, wellness-first lens. Instead of treating AI as a productivity mandate, participants will learn how to use AI as a tool for clarity, boundaries, and sustainable success. Using Helanah Warren's "Breathable Workday Framework," this interactive workshop demonstrates how AI can help UC staff reclaim time, reduce cognitive load, and create more space for the work that matters—without burnout, tech fatigue, or over-automation.Learning Outcomes: –How to use AI to streamline tasks like email, communication, planning, and documentation. –Scripts, prompts, and workflows that turn overwhelm into clarity. –Micro-boundaries that prevent AI from becoming "one more thing." –A 3-step model for integrating AI ethically and sustainably. –Somatic and mindset strategies to stay grounded during tech-driven change.Registrants will be sent a Zoom link and bCal invite as the virtual workshop date draws near.

events.title: Organic Chemistry Seminar
events.description: Hao Xu, Professor of Chemistry, Brandeis UniversitySearching for New Reactivity: Merging Enzymatic Catalysis with Iron Catalysis for Highly Stereoselective Glycosaminoglycan AssemblyComplex glycans are directly involved in essential life processes, but it is challenging to precisely assemble them in sufficient quantities with high homogeneity. One major hurdle is that the stereoselectivity in glycosylation often varies with substrates, thus it is difficult to develop an exquisitely selective glycosylation method that is also broadly effective. In particular, searching for a general solution for stereoselective assembly of 1,2-cis-glycosidic bonds is an unsolved challenge. The lecture will focus on the discovery of a mechanistically unique and generally applicable approach for exclusively 1,2-cis-selective glycosylation. In this lecture, we will also discuss a generally applicable glycosaminoglycan (GAG) assembly strategy by merging the catalytic power of sulfotransferases (SULTs) with two distinct iron-catalyzed glycosylation reactions that have been recently discovered in our lab. Every glycosidic linkage in heparan sulfate (HS) was assembled by one of these iron-catalyzed, entirely stereoselective glycosylation reactions. An array of sulfate groups that are essential to the functions of HS were installed at their desired locations via the SULT-controlled sulfation reactions.The Organic Seminar Series is sponsored by the William G. Dauben lecture fund

events.title: Student Faculty Macro Lunch: "Reconciling Treatment Effects Estimates across Levels of Aggregation"
events.description: Abstract: Empirical researchers often estimate treatment effects at different levels of aggregation to address confounding shocks or to detect violations of the stable unit treatment value assumption. Using eight widely used datasets on trade, employment, syndicated loans, patents, and stock holdings, we document that disaggregated data share common properties that complicate comparisons across aggregation levels. We show that, under standard specifications, these properties can lead treatment effect estimates to differ across levels of aggregation even in the absence of shocks or SUTVA violations. These gaps arise mechanically from implicit weighting across levels of aggregation, entry and exit, and Jensen's inequality. We characterize the conditions under which they become quantitatively important and propose simple approaches that are not sensitive to these sources of bias. Using practical examples, we show how aligning estimates across levels of aggregation can help researchers separately identify confounding shocks, spillovers, and extensive-margin changes at little additional cost.

events.title: CCB Seminar: Denis Titov - Using Math and Experiments to Study Metabolism
events.description: Abstract: My laboratory combines experiments and computation to develop a predictive understanding of metabolism—how it is regulated, why it is organized the way it is, and how it breaks down in aging and disease. We develop quantitative models and experimental tools to uncover the principles that govern metabolic behavior and to test their predictions in living systems. In this talk, I will describe how this approach has helped us address three longstanding puzzles in metabolism: why rapidly growing cells exhibit the Warburg Effect, what classical allosteric regulators of glycolysis actually do in cells, and how caloric restriction extends lifespan.

events.title: Operator Algebras Seminar: The Lima Bean Law
events.description: Speaker: Todd Kemp, University of California, San DiegoR-Diagonal elements are the most rotationally-invariant operators in free probability: a is R-diagonal if a has the same law as ua (and au) for any Haar unitary u freely independent from a. Examples include circular elements and Haar unitaries. They are the large-N limits of the most general kind of matrix with totally random eigenvectors; i.e. the (*-distribution) model is an ensemble of the form UAV where A is any matrix and U,V are Haar-distributed random matrices with {A,U,V} independent. One of the biggest modern theorems in random matrix theory, the Single Ring Theorem [Guionnet–Krishnapur–Zeitouni, 2011], proved that the density of eigenvalues of such a random matrix model converges to the Brown measure of the corresponding R-diagonal.In this talk I will discuss my recent work on "random walk" models of the form $(1+a_1)…(1+a_k)$ for freely independent R-diagonal elements $a_j$. We prove convergence of the density of eigenvalues for all these models as well. This talk will focus on the Brown measure of such shifted products, which we are able to describe quite precisely thanks to a surprising result (which I will discuss) on operator-valued freeness vs. scalar-valued freeness in the context of a symmetry we call "circulant invariance".Our main result is that, under diffusion rescaling, the Brown measure of any such k-step random walk superconverges to the large-N limit law of the standard Brownian motion on GL(N,C), yielding a very strong kind of Berger-Donsker scaling limit law (very strong because it holds even when the covariance of the terms is "wrong"). We call this scaling limit theorem The Lima Bean Law, for reasons that will become clear from pictures.This is joint work with Driver, Hall, Ho, Nemish, Nikitopoulos, and Parraud.

events.title: Esther's Army: The Christian Women Who Power the American Right
events.description: The 2024 election of Donald Trump was the culmination of the strategic efforts of Christian women over six decades. Observing Christian women's activism from grassroots networks to conservative academies and law school to public politics and jobs at the White House today���as they borrow feminist rhetoric to "lean in" to their executive skills while rejecting liberal feminism—Gaddini reveals how these women have turned being underestimated into a strategic force.Katie Gaddini is Associate Professor of Sociology at University College London. events.title: Physical Chemistry Seminar
events.description: Ahmad Omar, Assistant Professor, UC BerkeleyThe Statistical Mechanics of Active Interfaces, Bubbles, and Membranes Thermodynamics is among the most successful frameworks in the physical sciences because it explains how and why systems at or near equilibrium undergo dramatic transformations. Yet many living and active systems are sustained far from equilibrium, where the usual thermodynamic framework need not apply. In this talk, I will provide a broad overview of my group's efforts to develop a statistical-mechanical description of interfacial phenomena in such systems. Starting from microscopic dynamics and systematically coarse-graining to continuum fields, we recover analogues of familiar concepts such as surface tension and nucleation barriers, while revealing how activity and nonconservative forces modify them. I will show how this mechanical framework can describe the formation, fluctuations, and stability of active interfaces, bubbles, and membranes, comparing its predictions with simulations and experiments. Together, these results help clarify which equilibrium concepts remain useful far from equilibrium and how they must be generalized when they do.

events.title: Seminar 237 - Macroeconomics/Monetary Economics: "Artificial Intelligence and the Labor Market"
events.description: Abstract: We use advances in natural language processing to construct new measures of workers' tasklevel exposure to artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning from 2010 to 2023, capturing variation across firms, occupations, and time. Tasks with higher AI exposure subsequently experience reduced labor demand. To interpret these patterns, we develop a model that separates direct substitution from indirect reallocative effects of labor-saving technologies. Two variables summarize the impact of AI on within-firm labor demand: the mean exposure of an occupation's tasks, which depresses demand, and the concentration of exposure in a few tasks, which offsets losses by enabling workers to reallocate effort. Using an instrument based on historical university hiring networks, we find causal evidence consistent with these predictions. Despite strong substitution at the task level, overall employment effects are modest, as reduced demand in exposed occupations is offset by productivity-driven increases in labor demand at AI-adopting firms.

events.title: BAMPFA Exhibition: Private Frontiers: Media Legacies of the Cold War
events.description: On display from Sep 9 - Dec 13, 2026 | 11 am - 7 p.m. Bookended by the end of World War II in 1945 and the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, the Cold War was a transformative period in global history, marking both the end of the twentieth century and the waning of modernism. Though earlier historians defined the Cold War as the noncombative contest between the capitalist United States and the communist Soviet Union, recent interventions by scholars, artists, and writers have stressed that this period was also defined by the struggles for decolonization and national liberation movements across Asia and globally. Undeniable to the history of the Cold War is the crucial role that culture played in shaping perceptions of individuals, nations, and the global order, circulated through media such as international magazines, photographs, and television.Private Frontiers presents new and recent work in photography, video, and installation by contemporary artists who critically engage the Cold War as a prism for understanding today's media-saturated world. Through their methodologically-driven practices, artists Naeem Mohaiemen, Prajakta Potnis, TJ Shin, and Tiffany Sia draw on a range of references—including historical archives, news broadcasts, pop songs, and game theory—to critically examine media as a crucial arena in which politics was articulated and contested in the second half of the twentieth century. By looking carefully at how art and politics were entwined in the media of the past, these artists offer a way for us to carefully engage with the politics and art of our contemporary moment. events.title: Buchanan Lecture with Jenn Brophy | Programmable memory as a tool for plant genome engineering
events.description: Transkingdom transfer of DNA from Agrobacterium to plants is a stunning biological feat and the basis of the most widely used tool for introducing new DNA into plants. Yet despite decades of use, fundamental gaps remain in our understanding of Agrobacterium-mediated DNA transfer, particularly the dynamics and mechanisms of transferred DNA (T-DNA) integration into the plant genome. These gaps have limited our ability to reliably control transgene insertion. We developed T-SWITCH (T-DNA Sensing With Integrase CHassis), a transgenic Arabidopsis thaliana line that can be used to independently measure T-DNA delivery and integration after Agrobacterium-mediated transformation, to dissect these processes. Using T-SWITCH, we found that most transformation variables, including DNA repair factors, Agrobacterium virulence proteins, promoter choice, and vector architecture, act on T-DNA delivery, not integration. We find that ~17% of T-DNA delivery events do not result in T-DNA integration. Building on this insight, we use T-SWITCH to achieve integration-free genome editing, producing heritable mutations without Cas9 T-DNA in the genome in a single generation. In a related project we build synthetic genetic circuits that can sense and record specific biological events to achieve greater control over gene expression across the Arabidopsis root system. In Arabidopsis, a single primary root gives rise to secondary (lateral) roots, which subsequently branch into tertiary roots to form an increasingly complex root network over the plant's life. But because these branch types share the same core regulatory machinery, they have been impossible to control independently. We developed a synthetic genetic "counter" that can record repeated developmental events and enable independent control over gene expression across root types. The system successfully counts to two in heterozygous plants, and we discuss ongoing work to apply it for manipulation of root traits. Together, these systems show how synthetic circuits that record biological events can be used to understand or engineer previously inaccessible plant processes.

events.title: Demography Brown Bag Seminar with Mathew Hauer and Tyler McCormick: "AI in Demography"
events.description: Mathew E. Hauer is the Charles B. Nam Associate Professor of Sociology at Florida State University, Assistant Director of the Center for Demography and Population Health, and the Head of AI Agent Development at Aaru, a company focused on artificial intelligence and simulation (https://aaru.com/). His research lies at the intersection of demography, migration, population projections, and climate change, with particular expertise in modeling future population dynamics under climate stress. His work on climate migration and population vulnerability has earned numerous prestigious accolades, including the 2024 Early Achievement Award (https://www.populationassociation.org/about/annual-awards/early-achievement-award#:~:text=The%20Early%20Achievement%20award%20recognizes,scholars%20who%20received%20their%20Ph.) from the Population Association of America and the 2023 Cozzarelli Prize (http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/pnas-cozzarelli-2022.html) from the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, and is a finalist for the 2025 Cozzarelli Prize and the Max Planck-Humboldt Research Award. He is a two-time recipient of the E. Walter Terrie Award (https://www.sda-demography.org/Terrie-Award) for excellence in applied demography, and his dissertation on sea-level rise and human migration has accumulated over 1,500 citations since 2016. Dr. Hauer's research has significantly shaped our understanding of climate change's demographic impacts, from sea-level rise displacement to temperature extremes and coastal flooding. His work has been featured in over 800 media outlets worldwide, including the New York Times, The Guardian, Time Magazine, National Geographic, and the Washington Post. Before joining FSU, he spent nearly a decade directing the Applied Demography Program at the University of Georgia. Tyler McCormick's work develops statistical models for inference and prediction in scientific settings where data are sparsely observed or measured with error, with a particular focus on measuring and understanding human behavior. His recent projects include estimating features of social networks (e.g. the degree of clustering or how central an individual is) using data from standard surveys, inferring a likely cause of death (when deaths happen outside of hospitals) using reports from surviving caretakers, and quantifying & communicating uncertainty in predictive models for global health policymakers. He holds a Ph.D. in Statistics (with distinction) from Columbia University and is the recipient of the NIH Director's New Innovator Award, NIH Career Development (K01) Award, Army Research Office Young Investigator Program Award, and a Google Faculty Research Award. Currently, he is a Professor of Statistics and Sociology at the University of Washington, where he is also a core faculty member in the Center for Statistics and the Social Sciences and a Senior Data Science Fellow at the eScience Institute. During the 2019-2020 academic year Tyler was a Visiting Faculty Researcher at Google People+AI Research (PAIR). Tyler is the former Editor of the Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics (JCGS) and a Fellow of the American Statistical Association. Tyler is currently a member of the Committee on Applied and Theoretical Statistics at the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, & Medicine. More information on Tyler's work is here: https://thmccormick.github.io (https://thmccormick.github.io/).

events.title: Eva Odzuck | Plato's Critique of Democracy
events.description: This lecture reconstructs Plato's critique of the democratic concept of freedom in Books 8 and 9 of the Republic and argues that this critique is more context-sensitive, complex, and constructive than is generally assumed in current scholarship. The lecture argues that, in his analysis of democracy, Plato sheds light on the psychological, institutional, and conceptual dimensions of populism and its connection to tyranny—dimensions that could also be relevant to understanding the problems facing democracies today. Eva Helene Odzuck is Professor of Political Philosophy at the University of Regensburg. Her research focus is on ancient and early modern political thought and on liberal democracy. Eva Odzuck's monographs include „Thomas Hobbes' körperbasierter Liberalismus" (2016) and „Keimbahneingriffe im Namen der Freiheit?" (2026). Her research has been published in journals such as Hobbes Studies, History of European Ideas, Zeitschrift für Politikwissenschaft, Zeitschrift für praktische Philosophie, and The Review of Politics.If you require an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact ies@berkeley.edu with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days before the event.

events.title: Seminar 291, Department Seminar: Suresh Naidu (Columbia University) - The Economic Geography of American Slavery
events.description: Abstract: What would the antebellum American economy have looked like without slavery? Using new micro-data on the U.S. economy in 1860, we document that where free and enslaved workers live and how much they earn correlates strongly—but differently— with geographic proxies for agricultural productivity, disease, and ease of slave escape. To explain these patterns, we build a quantitative spatial model of slavery, where slaveholders coerce enslaved workers into supplying more labor, capture the proceeds of their labor, and assign them to sectors and occupations that maximize owner profits rather than worker welfare. Combining theory and data, we then quantify how dismantling the institution of slavery affected the spatial economy. We find that the economic impacts of emancipation are substantial, generating welfare gains for the enslaved of roughly 1,200%, while reducing welfare of free workers by 0.7% and eliminating slaveholder profit. Aggregate GDP rises by 9.1%, with a contraction in agricultural productivity counteracted by an expansion in manufacturing and services driven by an exodus of formerly enslaved workers out of agriculture and into the U.S. North.
