events.title: Josette Melchor // Newtemporary: Designing in the Space Between New and Next
events.description: The Jacobs Institute for Design Innovation welcomes Josette Melchor, founder and cultural strategist working across art, technology, cities, and responsible AI. As the founder of Gray Area and now Newtemporary — and a board member of the Burning Man Project — Josette has spent her career shaping experiences that connect emerging technologies with civic life, cultural infrastructure, and public imagination. Her work moves fluidly across spatial strategy, immersive media, curation, and systems thinking, always with an eye toward how culture and technology evolve together. ​In this talk, Josette will explore the idea behind Newtemporary, the notion that everything from culture to place to technology is always in transition. She will share how this perspective informs her work with cities, developers, and cultural organizations, from designing immersive experiences and public spaces to prototyping ethical and creative uses of AI. events.title: Berkeley Book Chat with Debarati Sanyal
events.description: Arts of the Border (Fordham, 2025) investigates the consequences of unfolding catastrophes across the world and the displacement they continue to produce. Through recent narratives and media representations of the refugee "crisis" at Europe's edges, it tells a new story about those on the move, the technologies unleashed on them at borders, the racialized and colonial histories that inform these technologies, and the artistry with which migrants and allies bear witness to displacement. The book reorients us toward the creativity and movement of migrants themselves — their "arts of the border" — as well as toward the political force of the arts that represent them, whether in literature, documentary film, or art installations.Debarati Sanyal (French) proposes kino-aesthetics as a framework for capture and fugitivity at borders. From kino (to set in motion) and aesthetics (relating to sensory perception), kino-aesthetics conveys the force of bodies in motion and the image in its circulation. Sanyal examines the simultaneity of capture and escape at thresholds of illegalization, from airport detention zones to Calais's "jungle" and the Euro-African border at Ceuta and Melilla. What emerges throughout these case studies is a portrayal of border violence in its racial and colonial forms as well as an archive of refusal, fugitivity, and un-bordered imagining. Sanyal is joined by Damon Young (Film & Media and French). After a brief discussion, they respond to questions from the audience.

events.title: Bioengineering Seminar: Single Cells in Context: A Dyad View that Bridges Single-Cell and Spatial Biology
events.description: Abstract: Single-cell sequencing has revolutionized cell atlases, but it is inherently context-poor: it catalogs cell states after dissociation, while many of the most important biological programs are relational: triggered by contact, proximity, or short-range signaling between specific partners. In this talk, I will present a dyad-centered framework and enabling technologies that treat cell–cell interactions as a measurable layer between single-cell and spatial biology. The central idea is simple: a cell's induced transcriptomic change in response to a partner cell is itself a quantitative readout of the partner's function. If one cell activates, suppresses, kills, rescues, or instructs another, the responder's state encodes information about what the first cell did, often more directly than measuring the first cell's basal transcriptome alone. I will describe our Lab-on-a-Particle platform, which creates millions of standardized microscale assay environments compatible with conventional workflows and downstream sequencing. Using Nanovials, cavity-containing hydrogel microparticles with selectively functionalized interiors, we can capture secreted proteins and binding events while keeping cells viable—enabling secretion-encoded functional screening followed by recovery for single-cell RNA-seq and targeted sequence identification. Building on this, I will introduce Cell-Cell-seq, which uses nanovials to co-compartmentalize defined cell pairs and couple dyad-specific functional measurements with transcriptomic profiling of a composite induced dyad-level transcriptome. By comparing paired interactions to matched single-cell controls, we can isolate interaction-induced programs, infer directionality, and map how heterogeneous immune and tumor populations engage. Together, these approaches provide a scalable route to connect function, interaction context, and molecular identity, offering a practical bridge from dissociated single-cell genomics toward the contextual logic needed for predictive multicellular biology and therapeutic discovery.

events.title: Charting Your Path in a Changing World: Using Creativity & Innovation to Shape What's Next (2026 Fall NOW Encore Series)
events.description: 2026 NOW Encore Series (https://hr.berkeley.edu/development/career-development/workshops) In a time of ongoing change across higher education and public service, the ability to anticipate, adapt, and move forward with intention has become essential. This highly engaging 75-minute virtual session invites UC Berkeley staff to explore how their creative and innovative capacities can help them chart a meaningful, resilient path - regardless of role, function, or career stage. Participants will explore how to shift from prediction to anticipation, using future-forward thinking to expand possibilities while remaining grounded in UC's mission. The session emphasizes change agility in practice: recognizing signals that it may be time to pivot, letting go of perfection in favor of progress, and using learning, not failure, as feedback. Through real-world examples, guided reflection, and practical application, participants will identify small, intentional actions that build readiness and momentum, even amid uncertainty.Learning Outcomes: –Differentiate between prediction and anticipation and use anticipation as a practical, future-forward approach for navigating complexity and uncertainty in their work. –Recognize signals that indicate when to adapt or pivot, reframing change and learning as sources of insight that strengthen change agility rather than as disruption or failure. –Apply creative and innovative thinking to take one meaningful next action, making progress without waiting for perfect conditions while remaining aligned with UC's mission.Registrants will be sent a Zoom link and bCal invite as the virtual workshop date draws near.

events.title: IPSR Colloquium: Ariana Castro, Matthew Elliott, and Nathalia Carvalho
events.location: Room 1102 Berkeley Way West, 2121 Berkeley Way, Berkeley, CA 94704, USA
events.description: Matthew V. ElliottPostdoctoral ScholarDepartment of PsychologyUniversity of California, BerkeleyExperiential and Physiological Measures of Emotion Distancing in Self-Injurious Thoughts and Behaviors.Self-injurious thoughts and behaviors (SITBs) are often motivated by efforts to alleviate distressing emotions, yet the distinct roles of emotion reactivity and regulation are difficult to disentangle. We examined these processes during an emotion distancing task using multimodal measures of subjective emotional experience, autonomic physiology (pupillometry and skin conductance), and functional MRI, and tested their associations with suicidal ideation, nonsuicidal self-injury, and suicide attempts. Emotion reactivity showed limited associations with SITBs across subjective, peripheral physiological, and neural measures. In contrast, regulation-related pupillary and posterior cingulate cortex responses were associated with suicidal ideation, recurrent nonsuicidal self-injury, and lifetime suicide attempt burden, although patterns varied across clinical outcomes. Overall, findings more consistently implicated difficulties with emotion regulation than heightened reactivity and highlighted sensitive physiological measures that may point to specific neural systems for further study.Dr. Matthew Elliott is a postdoctoral scholar in Clinical Science at the University of California, Berkeley, working under the mentorship of Prof. Sheri Johnson. Prior to his postdoc, he completed his PhD in Clinical Science at UC Berkeley and his predoctoral clinical internship through the UC San Diego/VA San Diego Psychology Internship Training Program. His research investigates how challenges to emotional and circadian regulation contribute to vulnerability for mania, impulsivity, and self-injury. Dr. Elliott's work integrates careful clinical characterization, experimental methods, and peripheral and central physiological measures to better understand mechanisms of clinical risk.Ariana Andrea Castro LeonPostdoctoral Research FellowDepartment of PsychologyUniversity of California, BerkeleyEmotion and Reasoning in Mania: Effects of Internal and External Emotion on Analogical ReasoningEmotion changes how people process information, including during analogicalreasoning, a process involved in learning across domains and, ultimately, meaningmaking. Previous research indicates that external emotional information enhancesanalogical reasoning when it is task-relevant and impairs it when it is task-irrelevant.Internal emotional states amplify some of these effects. The present research examinedwhether the effects of external and internal emotion on analogical reasoning vary as afunction of hypomanic traits. Results may inform our understanding of how emotioninfluences thinking processes relevant to bipolar disorder.Dr. Castro is a Postdoctoral Research Fellow in the UC Berkeley CALM Program. Thegoal of her research is to inform models of how and why psychopathology emerges,with a focus on the role of emotional processes. Her work has developed along twointerconnected lines of research. First, she examines how emotion influences analogicalreasoning, a process through which people identify patterns and form beliefs aboutthemselves, the world, and the future. Second, she studies broader emotion-cognitiondynamics across different forms of psychopathology (e.g., how contentment maydifferentiate internalizing symptoms). She is currently examining the role of analogicalreasoning in mania within the CALM Program. She is also expanding the scope of herresearch by studying motivation, emotion-related impulsivity, and suicidality.Nathalia CarvalhoPostdoctoral ScholarDepartment of PsychologyUC Berkeley;Assistant Professor at Pontifical Catholic University of Rio de Janeiro, Psychology DepartmentThe Effects of Individual and Shared Awe on Romantic Relationship QualityAwe is a complex emotional response characterized by feelings of wonder, perceived vastness, and a need for cognitive accommodation. It is often accompanied by a diminished sense of self and a heightened sense of connection to something larger than oneself. Previous research suggests that awe can promote prosocial behavior, in part by reducing self-focus and increasing orientation toward others. Despite these interpersonal consequences, relatively little research has examined awe's role within close relationships. The primary goal of the present study was therefore to examine whether experiencing awe individually or with a romantic partner is associated with romantic relationship quality, and whether shared awe is associated with greater relationship quality than individual awe. We also examined whether these associations vary as a function of theoretically relevant relationship processes, particularly self-expansion and inclusion of the other in the self.Nathalia Carvalho earned her PhD in Psychology from Pontifical Catholic University of Rio de Janeiro, in Brazil, in 2024. She is currently an assistant professor at the same university and earned an unpaid leave in 2026 to work as a postdoctoral researcher at the University of California, Berkeley.

events.title: William Ludington: Molecular basis of microbiome-host specificity through selective adhesion
events.description: Animals throughout the Metazoa selectively acquire commensal gut bacteria that promote host fitness, yet the mechanisms by which hosts recruit specific symbionts from the environment remain poorly understood. Current models suggest that gut bacteria use nonspecific adhesins to bind host tissues that overlap with their nutritional niche, resulting in proliferation. In contrast, we found that symbiotic lactobacilli in Drosophila melanogaster adhere with high affinity to a spatially defined subregion of the foregut. We identified the bacterial proteins that they are necessary and sufficient to localize symbiotic bacteria to the foregut niche. Bioinformatics analyses indicate a conserved colonization island with diversified receptors throughout the Firmicutes, including commensals and pathogens spanning the Lactobacillales and Clostridia. We are now using the genetic tools available in Drosophila to define the host genetic basis for this selective colonization niche.Division(s): Divisions of Biochemistry, Biophysics & Structural Biology, Division of Cell Biology, Development & Physiology, and Genetics, Genomics, Evolution & Development

events.title: CLIMB + Neyman Seminar with Daniela Witten: Testing hypothesis via orthogonalization
events.description: Please join us for a joint CLIMB + Neyman Seminar with Daniela Witten Testing hypothesis via orthogonalization Abstract Classical hypothesis testing frameworks break down in contemporary settings in which null hypotheses are increasingly abstract, the same data are used to both generate and test hypotheses, and minimal assumptions about the underlying data are made. In this work, we propose a new framework for conducting valid hypothesis tests in broad contexts. We propose to add and subtract external noise generated from a symmetric shift-family to our data, X, to partition it into two pieces, X1 and X2. We provide a generic strategy for orthogonalizing X2 against X1 under the null hypothesis H0, then show that testing whether the orthogonalization was successful provides a valid test of H0 under mild assumptions. Remarkably, this framework extends naturally to the post-selection inference setting with minimal modifications: we simply select a hypothesis on X1, then perform orthogonalization under the selected null. As our approach neither requires pre-specification of the selection mechanism, nor is restricted to a small class of data-generating distributions, it dramatically expands the settings for which valid post-selection inference can be conducted. We showcase the flexibility of our proposal in a number of case studies. This is joint work with Ameer Dharamshi (McGill University) and Runjia Zou (University of Washington). Bio Daniela Witten is a professor of Statistics and Biostatistics at University of Washington, and the Dorothy Gilford Endowed Chair in Mathematical Statistics. She develops statistical machine learning methods for high-dimensional data, with a focus on unsupervised learning. She has received a number of awards for her research in statistical machine learning: most notably the Spiegelman Award from the American Public Health Association for a (bio)statistician under age 40, and the Presidents' Award from the Committee of Presidents of Statistical Societies for a statistician under age 41. Daniela is a co-author of the textbook "Introduction to Statistical Learning", and has served as Joint Editor of Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B. CLIMB Voleon Seminars are organized by the Center for the Theoretical Foundations of Learning, Inference, Information, Intelligence, Mathematics, and Microeconomics at Berkeley (CLIMB (https://climb.berkeley.edu/)), and are generously supported by the Voleon Group. CLIMB addresses new conceptual and mathematical challenges arising at the interface between technology, science, and society.If you require an accommodation for effective communication or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact Naomi Yamasaki at climb-support@eecs.berkeley.edu or 510-710-8488 with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days before the event.

events.title: Film Screening: Barbara Forever
events.description: "Pioneering lesbian filmmaker . . . Barbara Hammer takes center stage in Brydie O'Connor's Teddy Award-winning debut feature. . . . Throughout her monumental career, Hammer made over ninety moving-image works that often centered on her own life, body, and lovers . . . when such life-affirming, honest depictions of sapphic people were scarce. Bolstered by exquisitely edited archival footage, this beautifully intimate documentary assembles an equally lyrical portrait of the visual poet, illuminating how Hammer's legacy continues to inspire artists and preserve our shared histories. At the same time, it never loses sight of the ambitious, funny, bold, and joyful woman at its center" (Kate Bove, Frameline).

Knowing your numbers is one of the best ways to evaluate your health by identifying your risk and providing motivation for managing your health. Thank you so much for this service. It is invaluable. I'll be back next year to check again and make sure I stay on track."

events.title: Heather Christofk: Metabolic Regulation of Cell State
events.description: Our research focuses on the relationship between metabolism and cell state. We began by studying how metabolism changes during different cell state transitions – during malignant transformation, stem cell differentiation, and virus infection. However, our work has suggested a more bidirectional relationship between metabolism and cell state, whereby metabolism is not only altered during cell state transitions, but metabolic changes can also drive them. Here, I will present examples of our recent and ongoing work in three different areas of study: tissue stem cell metabolism, developmental metabolism, and cancer metabolism. I will highlight efforts to translate our findings to the clinic, new tools and methodologies we are developing to better study cell type-specific metabolism in vivo, and new questions we are answering focused on the impact of metabolism on cell state transitions in varied biological contexts.Division(s): MTx (Molecular Therapeutics)

events.title: Bancroft Library Roundtable
events.description: The Port of Los Angeles is the United States' busiest shipping port, connecting California to the nation and Americans to a rapidly changing globe. In A Machine to Move Ocean and Earth (Norton, 2024), author James Tejani traces the port's present-day importance to origins deep within the nation's past: westward expansion, the annexation of the Hispanic Southwest, political conflict over slavery, and the beginnings of U.S. global power. Tejani's talk will examine this story through three Bay Area residents: the frontier government scientist George Davidson; Army Capt. Edward Ord; and pathbreaking engineer-inventor A.W. Von Schmidt.

events.title: REI Colloquium: Banished Citizens: A History of the Mexican American Women Who Endured Repatriation
events.description: From 1921 to 1944, approximately one million ethnic Mexicans living in the United States were removed across the border to Mexico. What officials called "repatriation" was in fact banishment: 60 percent of those expelled were US citizens, mainly working-class women and children whose husbands and fathers were Mexican immigrants. Drawing on transnational archival sources, oral histories, and private collections, Banished Citizens illuminates the lasting effects of coerced mass removal on three generations of ethnic Mexicans. Ramírez argues that banishment served interests on both sides of the border. In the United States, the government accused ethnic Mexicans of dependence on social services to justify removal, thereby scapegoating them for post-World War I and Depression-era economic woes. In Mexico, meanwhile, officials welcomed returnees for their potential to bolster the labor force. In the process, all Mexicans in the United States—citizens and undocumented immigrants alike—were cast as financially burdensome and culturally foreign. Shedding particular light on the experiences of banished women expelled under claims of their likelihood to become a public charge and links to the outdated coverture doctrine, Ramírez demonstrates that US-citizen women and children were targeted as a strategy to banish entire mixed-status families. Nonetheless, banished women courageously and resiliently fought for decades to reclaim their US citizenship and return to their native country. Nevertheless, banishment often interrupted their ability to pass on US citizenship to their children, robbed their families of generational wealth, and drastically slowed upward mobility. Today, their descendants continue to confront and resist the impact of these injustices-and are breaking the silence to ensure that this history is not forgotten. This is an accessible event. If you have accessibility needs and need reasonable accommodations to participate they will be provided. For more information, and to make a request, please contact Ezra Bristow at ezrabristow@berkeley.edu

events.title: A pelagic paradox: the rise and fall of large animals with shells in the pelagic realm
events.description: In contrast to the benthos, where mineralized exoskeletons have proliferated and become increasing well protected over time, the pelagic realm shows first an increase, then a post-Cretaceous decline in large animals with shells. The pelagic realm therefore diverged from the benthos after the Cretaceous, and also shows a divergence within the realm between large and small organisms with respect to mineralization. This example illustrates a widespread phenomenon of phenotypic obsolescence through time.

events.title: The Once and Future World Order: Why Global Civilization Will Survive the Decline of the West
events.description: The Once and Future World Order: Why Global Civilization Will Survive the Decline of the West Thursday, September 17, 2026 12:30 ��� 2 pm *Lunchtime talk* Institute of International Studies 223 Philosophy HallREGISTER (https://forms.gle/k1UvS6pJUuwKDPXR7) The Institute of International Studies (http://iis.berkeley.edu/) & the Goldman School of Public Policy (http://gspp.berkeley.edu/) are pleased to welcome Prof. Amitav Acharya (https://www.american.edu/sis/faculty/aacharya.cfm) for a public talk at IIS. Since the dawn of the twenty-first century, the West has been in crisis. Social unrest, political polarization, and the rise of other great powers—especially China—threaten to unravel today's Western-led world order. Many fear this would lead to global chaos. But the West has never had a monopoly on order. Surveying five thousand years of global history, political scientist Amitav Acharya reveals that world order—the political architecture enabling cooperation and peace among nations—existed long before the rise of the West. Moving from ancient Sumer, India, Greece, and Mesoamerica, through medieval caliphates and Eurasian empires into the present, Acharya shows that humanitarian values, economic interdependence, and rules of inter-state conduct emerged across the globe over millennia. History suggests order will endure even as the West retreats. In fact, the end of Western dominance offers us the opportunity to build a better world, where non-Western nations find more voice, power, and prosperity. Instead of fearing the future, the West should learn from history and cooperate with the Rest to forge a more equitable order.

events.title: (Screening) GAAVANI | Celebrating the Female Voice in Gurbani Kirtan
events.description: Join us for a screening of GAAVANI (https://www.gaavani.com/), a film that marks a significant moment in Sikh history. For the first time in 556 years since the founding of the Sikh faith, 31 women travel across northern India to sing Kirtan in all 31 primary musical raags of the Guru Granth Sahib at sacred sites. This film captures breathtaking cinematography, soul-stirring soundscapes, while exploring how these women serve as vital carriers of wisdom, faith and strength - bringing 556 years of legacy into a sharp, contemporary and lived focus. The screening will be followed by a conversation with filmmaker Navpreet Kaur. The event will be moderated by Puninder Singh (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/people/puninder-singh), the Sabharwal Lecturer in Sikh Studies at UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Thu, September 17, 2026 TIME: 5-7 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall REGISTRATION: The event is FREE but a reservation is required. Please reserve your seat HERE (https://www.eventbrite.com/e/gaavani-film-california-premiere-rsvp-berkeley-tickets-1994097467204?aff=oddtdtcreator) —————-SYNOPSIS:GAAVANI: Her Journey Home (https://www.gaavani.com/) follows a diverse group of 31 women—teachers, students, mothers, and community members—as they journey across northern India to perform Kirtan in the 31 primary raags of the Guru Granth Sahib. From the busy streets of Delhi to historic shrines in Amritsar and beyond, the film captures both the challenges and triumphs of this groundbreaking effort. The film explores the relationship between practice, music, gender, and lived spiritual experience. Featuring insights from scholars and speakers such as Dr. Gurnam Singh and Jessi Kaur, GAAVANI (https://www.gaavani.com/) reflects on the "female orientation" of the soul in Sikh philosophy and highlights the deep spiritual significance of sung devotion. The film also honors the role of male mentors and allies who supported this movement, presenting a vision of a community in which women and men are empowered to participate fully in the Guru's Shabad. As a legacy project, GAAVANI (https://www.gaavani.com/) seeks to inspire Sikh children and adults to discover their own musical connection to Gurbani Kirtan and to help ensure that this sacred art form continues to thrive for future generations. Running time 47 minutes. See the trailer HERE (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pyeqlAeNi9Q) About the Filmmaker: Navpreet Kaur is a dedicated community leader and media producer based in the San Francisco Bay Area. As a key founder of GAAVANI (https://www.gaavani.com/), she has spearheaded global and local initiatives to raise the female voice in Gurbani Kirtan. With a background in project leadership and a passion for deep personal discovery, Navpreet coordinated the historic 31-women Kirtan tour of northern India and served as the visionary and driving force behind the film production. Her work focuses on bridging Sikh spiritual wisdom and traditions with modern and meaningful community, educational and media platforms.About the moderator:Puninder Singh (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/people/puninder-singh) completed his PhD in Linguistic Anthropology at the University of Michigan in 2024. His work broadly examines how language and ideas about language mediate religious experience, particularly in the Sikh tradition. His current work examines the development of a new Sikh intellectual formation between 1920-1940, after the era of the Singh Sabha reform movement. He is also at work on several projects that examine how the Sikh tradition has engaged in dialogic and interactive relations with those around it, both linguistically and otherwise, in the long durée, from the early modern through the contemporary period. He is currently the Sabharwal Lecturer in Sikh Studies at the University of California, Berkeley.Event Poster ��————— Event is FREE and OPEN to the public. events.description: Since Donald Trump's reelection, universities have found themselves caught between principle and self-preservation. Should they stand up and risk getting cut down, or stay low and hope to escape the crossfire? For Professor Claudia Polsky, it was never a question. Determined to confront the administration's assault on higher education, she spearheaded a class action suit that has, so far, restored nearly a billion dollars in research funding to UC scientists and scholars. The litigation is ongoing. Join California editor Pat Joseph in conversation with Professor Claudia Polsky about the ongoing threats to American science and research, the rule of law, and what it means to fight back. CLAUDIA POLSKY Claudia Polsky is a clinical professor at Berkeley Law and the founding director of its Environmental Law Clinic. A former Deputy Attorney General at the California Department of Justice and litigator at Earthjustice and Public Citizen, she spent eighteen years in public-interest environmental law and has argued cases up to the U.S. Supreme Court. She has testified before Congress, and her clinic's victories include successful litigation against the federal government. ABOUT CALIFORNIA LIVE! events.title: A Roundtable on the History of the Far-Right in the US
events.description: Over the past decade, the far right has moved from the margins of American politics to its center. In turn, the topic now transcends the margins of historical scholarship to become a thriving field of inquiry. This roundtable brings together contributors to the Journal of Right-Wing Studies' two-part special issue, "The Far Right in US History (https://jrws.berkeley.edu/issues)," to discuss recent discoveries in the field. Drawing on work that spans conservative Catholic political thought, maternal activism on the right, the transnational circulation of white supremacist violence, Klan electoral politics, American monarchism, and the deep roots of Christian nationalism, panelists will consider what is gained by treating the far right as a subject of history rather than a contemporary aberration, and what remains stubbornly hard to study. How do historians define the "far right?" When does the radical become ordinary? And what do the archives allow us to see about movements with few formal records? Please join Professors Olivier Burtin (Université de Picardie Jules Verne) and Kathryn Olmsted (UC Davis), our distinguished guest editors, as they moderate a discussion on topics in the special issue. Authors and Discussants: -Mary Byrne (Rutgers) - "Moms for Liberty and the Legacy of White Maternalist Activism: Gendered Power and Cultural Organizing in Far-Right Movements" -Faith Lazar (Yale) - "If a Bomb Goes Off in the Woods: Preemptive Counterterrorism and the FBI Sting that Triggered Ruby Ridge" -Kyle Burke (University of South Florida) - "'A Planet-Wide Race War': The Global Circulation of White Supremacist Violence in the Late Twentieth Century" -Chelsea Ebin (Drew) - "Mapping the Influence of Conservative Catholic Political Thought on the American Right" Part 1 of the special issue is available and open access; Look for Part 2, out soon!

events.title: Irregular Labor Supply and Coordination in the Workplace: Experimental Evidence from India | Shreya Chandra
events.description: Job Market PresentationAbstract This paper studies how irregular labor supply affects the organization of production in the context of a large apparel manufacturing cluster in India. Production is organized as batch processing lines, where tasks are performed sequentially to produce the finished product. In the status quo, workers choose their own work timings, resulting in significant dispersion in arrival times at the firm. I conduct an experiment with 96 small factories comprising 600 workers, where all workers in treatment firms are incentivized to arrive at work by the owner's preferred start time for a period of 4-weeks. Workers are paid a daily bonus equivalent to 20% of average earnings if they arrive on or before the start time. Incentives increase timely arrival in treatment firms by 43% relative to control firms. These changes are driven by workers who were consistently late to arrive at the firm at baseline. As a result, there is meaningful improvement in coordination of worker arrival times – dispersion in arrival times decreases by 17%. Individual worker output increase for all workers in treatment firms, not only those who changed their arrival times as a result of the incentive. I show that these positive spillovers are generated through gains along the production line from improved coordination. Weekly firm output increases by 29% and delays in order-completion fall by 13 percentage points.

events.title: Music Studies Colloquium: Cesar Favila (UCLA)
events.description: The Franciscan Missionary Voice in Late-Colonial New SpainCesar Favila (UCLA) Throughout the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, the Franciscan Order in New Spain published small books containing missionary songs for convincing nominal Catholics to confess their sins and amend their lives. While musicologists and historians have focused on the effectiveness of missionary music in the conversion of Indigenous people with no prior knowledge of Christianity, the musical implications of the Franciscan missions of spiritual renewal to the "faithful" in the centuries that followed the conquest of New Spain remain understudied. This talk explores the contents of these songbooks and the broader missionary context, revealing a Franciscan awareness of the effectiveness of song, aurality, orality, and voice to understand divine presence and to convey the Church's post-Tridentine sacramental and reconciliatory messages that aimed at maintaining a faithful citizenry in Spanish territories. This talk also demonstrates how this missionary process provided for the Franciscans to imitate Christ through voice and reveals the voice as a medium for sacramental expression. A reception will follow.

events.title: GIANTS RISING Film Screening in the Redwood Grove
events.description: A very special outdoor film screening amongst the redwoods! Experience the award-winning documentary film GIANTS RISING (https://www.giantsrising.com/) under towering redwood trees, with featured redwood researcher Dr. Todd Dawson.Movie-goers can enjoy special pre-movie after-hours in the UC Botanical Garden (5:00-6:30pm), exploring our collections of plants from around the world, including all three of the world's redwoods–California's giant sequoias, coast redwoods, and the dawn redwoods of Asia. Bring a picnic dinner to enjoy before the movie!Then head to our historic Redwood Grove outdoor amphitheater for an inspiring talk about these iconic trees with UC Berkeley professor of Integrative Biology Dr. Todd Dawson. Redwood Grove Gate opens just before 6:30pm. Film projection begins at sundown, approx. 7:00pm.Don't miss this perfect film experience celebrating redwoods on screen and in person! ABOUT THE MOVIEGIANTS RISING (https://www.giantsrising.com/)The secrets and superpowers of the redwoods Lisa Landers | USA, 2024 | 82 minutes Language: English (minimal Yurok)GIANTS RISING takes you on an unparalleled adventure through the towering majesty of California's redwood forests, crafting a narrative that's rich and as deep as the woods it explores. The film stands out in the documentary genre, breaking the mold with its heartfelt homage to these ancient sentinels […] The blend of scientific exploration and emotional, artistic depth paints a vivid picture of the redwoods, positioning them as natural marvels and central figures in our environmental dialogue." A journey into the heart of America's most iconic forests, GIANTS RISING explores the secrets, superpowers and saga of the redwoods— the tallest and some of the oldest living beings on Earth. It's an epic tale that reveals the wonders of these majestic trees and our dramatic, ever-evolving relationship with them. Living links to the past, redwoods also hold powers that may play a role in our future, including their ability to withstand fire and capture carbon, to offer clues about resilience, and even to enhance our own well-being. Through the voices of biologists, artists, Native communities and others, we discover the redwoods' scientific marvels and our deep cultural ties to them. It's a story that offers insights about the value of our interconnections, and the promise of solutions that will help us ALL rise up to face the challenges that lay ahead. "GIANTS RISINGis a powerful educational tool—stunningly filmed, deeply rooted in science, and highly engaging. I've witnessed firsthand how this expertly woven tapestry of stories captivates both students and lifelong learners, while sparking critical conversations about our relationship to redwoods, to all forests, and to the natural world." - Dr. Todd Dawson, Professor of Environmental Science at the University of California, Berkeley

events.title: Film Screening: Contempt
events.description: In Italy, Fritz Lang is shooting The Odyssey for an American producer (Jack Palance). Fritz mourns classical culture but will settle for swords and sandals; like The Odyssey, Contempt is about man against circumstances, and such is the circumstance of cinema. The screenwriter, Paul (Michel Piccoli), meanwhile, becomes lost in Rome, and during his odyssey, his wife, Camille (Brigitte Bardot), enters into a crisis of contempt. Contempt becomes very much Camille/Penelope's story as, on Paul's return, their marriage is dissected. With its colors and compositions, its ruins, its vistas, and especially its movement, Contempt is epic, but it is an epic stripped bare by its director.

events.description: In Taipei there are only seven days in the year 2000, the rain just keeps pouring, a mysterious plague makes people act like roaches, quarantine zones are everywhere, and even the most alienated urbanite dreams dance numbers from 1950s Hong Kong films. Such is the end of the millennium as pictured by Tsai Ming-liang in this part-musical, part-sci-fi exploration of modern isolation, environmental catastrophe, and the failure of communication. The film's apocalyptic Blade Runneratmosphere fits surprisingly well with Tsai's auteurist vision of societal and emotional collapse, as does its pathetically realistic musical numbers, inspired by the films of popular 1950s songstress Grace Chang.

events.title: Film Screening: Bellissima
events.description: "What is acting after all?" Maddalena (Anna Magnani) rhetorically asks before the mirror in Luchino Visconti's melodrama of mother love and misplaced ambition. Magnani's extraordinary performance is its own answer. As a working-class mother desperate to get her young daughter a shot at stardom through a Cinecittà casting call, Magnani turns what might have been a simplistic caricature of a domineering stage mother into a fully rendered character, both hilarious and tragically human. Visconti's direction similarly refuses to distinguish between satire and sincerity; even while it mocks the business of moviemaking, Bellissima is an exquisite example of the filmmaker's craft.

events.title: Film Screening: The Last Waltz
events.description: Martin Scorsese grew up listening to seminal rock DJ Alan Freed, and from Mean Streets onward, his movies have been driven by the power of rock and roll. His love of music is innate and instinctual, so when The Band decided to hang it up after seventeen years on the road, they chose Scorsese to film their farewell concert at Winterland Ballroom on Thanksgiving 1976. The film intercuts the glorious music from one of the all-time great concert lineups with interviews with members of The Band as they talk about their lives and music. The Last Waltz is an elegiac masterpiece that captures a special moment in music history.

events.title: Probabilistic Operator Algebra Seminar: Fermionic optimal transport
events.location: to attend via Zoom email David Jekel (daj@math.ku.dk) remote on-line talk
events.description: Speaker: Paola Zurlo, Universita degli Studi Aldo Moro, Bari, ItalyWe consider optimal transport between quantum dynamical systems on $Z _2 $- graded von Neumann algebras. In the usual, non-graded setting, Wasserstein distances between quantum systems can be defined in terms of transport plans on tensor products involving the commutant of one of the algebras. We briefly recall this construction and describe its extension to the graded setting, where the usual commutant and tensor product are replaced by the twisted commutant and the Fermi tensor product. The main point of the construction is a correspondence between fermionic and usual transport plans. More precisely, using cyclic representations associated with transport plans and the Klein isomorphisms induced by the gradings, we establish a one-to-one correspondence between fermionic transport plans and graded transport plans in the usual tensor product. This correspondence allows the Wasserstein distances in the fermionic setting to be related to the corresponding distances in the non-graded setting, and in particular yields their metric properties.

events.title: Vivien Schmidt | The Power of Ideas and Discourse in Political Analysis—and its applications to Europe
events.description: Vivien Schmidt's new book, The Power of Ideas and Discourse in Political Analysis: A Discursive Institutionalist Perspective (Oxford 2026) provides a sweeping appraisal of how ideas and discourse are used by policymakers and everyday citizens to understand the world, communicate with one another, and mobilize for collective action. It illustrates using examples of scholarly work on capitalism and democracy, international diplomacy and human rights, environmental, economic, and social policy, conservativism, neoliberalism, socialism, and populism. In so doing, the book also provides a discursive institutionalist perspective on the (constructivist) nature of meaning, the dynamics of change and the exercise of power. At a time of major political upheaval, with populism and authoritarianism on the rise, understanding agents' ideas and discourse is even more essential today than ever. The talk will illustrate with examples from the European Union and Europe more generally, both in terms of substantive issues and methodological approaches.Vivien A. Schmidt is Jean Monnet Professor of European Integration, Professor Emerita of International Relations and Political Science, and Founding Director of the Center for the Study of Europe at Boston University. She is Visiting Fellow at the European University Institute and Honorary Professor at LUISS University. Recent books include The Power of Ideas and Discourse in Political Analysis: A Discursive Institutionalist Perspective (Oxford 2026) and the award-winning Europe's Crisis of Legitimacy: Governing by Rules and Ruling by Numbers in the Eurozone (Oxford 2020). Schmidt is a member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, a Chevalier in the French Legion of Honor, and a recipient of the Lifetime Achievement Award of the European Union Studies Association, an Honorary Doctorate from the Free University of Brussels, and a Guggenheim Foundation Fellowship. events.title: The 2nd Workshop on Governance and Policy in East Asia
events.location: IEAS Conference Room (2111 Bancroft Way, 5th Floor)
events.description: This workshop brings together scholars in public administration, political science, and public policy to examine governance and policy in Japan and East Asia from a variety of perspectives. The presentations cover a wide range of contemporary issues, including responses to declining birthrates, health policy, criminal justice policy, and political reporting, offering insights into how governments, political institutions, and societies respond to changing social and political challenges. A central aim of the workshop is to foster dialogue across different areas of research. Rather than limiting discussion to highly specialized debates within each field, presenters will introduce the broader questions that motivate their research, share their approaches and findings with scholars working on different topics, and discuss their wider implications. English and Japanese will be used flexibly throughout the workshop, allowing participants to exchange ideas in either language and encouraging open and accessible discussion across disciplinary and linguistic boundaries. By bringing different research areas and perspectives into conversation with one another, the workshop seeks to create opportunities for participants to discover new perspectives, make connections across fields, and develop a broader understanding of governance and policy in Japan and East Asia.Speakers:Ito, Masatsugu (Tokyo Metropolitan University) Matsubara, Hideyo (Konan University) Naito, Horoko (Institute of Developing Economies) Maeda, Takahiro (University of the Ryukyus) Mitani, Soichiro (Konan University)

events.title: Polly Fordyce: "Using microfluidics for high-throughput and quantitative biophysics and biochemistry"
events.description: Macromolecular interactions drive all biological processes: proteins bind DNA and RNA to regulate transcription and translation, dense networks of protein-protein interactions convey cellular signals, and enzyme-substrate interactions allow all of the chemical transformations essential for metabolism and signaling. The strength of these interactions predicts the timing and identity of downstream responses; therefore, quantitative biophysical and biochemical measurements are critical to decipher these networks, predict how they are disrupted in disease, and manipulate them for therapeutic purposes. Here, I will discuss the development of and results from several new microfluidic platforms that make it possible to acquire quantitative biochemical and biophysical data in vitro for thousands to millions of sequence variants in parallel.

events.title: Provincializing National Literatures: Soviet Literary Universalism and Georgian Alternatives
events.description: How can a literary system celebrate cultural diversity while quietly organizing it into a hierarchy? This talk explores that contradiction through the Soviet project of "multinational literature." At its center is the six-volume History of Multinational Soviet Literature (1970��1974), which presented the literatures of the USSR as equal parts of a common whole while positioning Russian literature as the privileged route to universality. Georgia reveals both the power and the limits of this model. Through Georgii Lomidze, Akaki Bakradze, and Guram Dochanashvili, the talk traces three competing visions of literary belonging: imperial integration, national self-assertion, and a transnational republic of readers. At stake is a larger question: Who gets to define the universal—and what happens to literatures forced to reach it through an imperial center?Zaal Andronikashvili is Professor of Cultural Studies at Ilia State University in Tbilisi and a Research Fellow at the Leibniz Center for Literary and Cultural Research (ZfL) in Berlin. A literary scholar and cultural historian, he works on empire, modernity and the cultural histories of the Soviet and post-Soviet worlds, with a particular focus on Georgia and the South Caucasus. His research rethinks European and global cultural history from the perspective of regions conventionally treated as peripheral, asking how imperial and national frameworks shape literary and cultural fomations. He has published widely in German, English, and Georgian.

events.title: Lara Fabian (UCLA), "The Caspian Corridor and the Making of a Connected Eurasia"
events.description: In this talk, I explore what happened when expanding empires from Iran and the Mediterranean world met the "circumcaspian system"—a constellation of patterns of mobility, exchange, and interaction that played out around the Caspian Sea over millennia. This framework helps us to see the processes that brought supra-regional powers into ever deeper contact with the diverse communities of the Caspian Sea territories. Moreover, it calls our attention to the network standards that developed as a result of imperial expansion. These norms made sociopolitical actors in the space increasingly legible to one another, facilitating increased cooperation as well as competition. To illustrate this process, I draw on multi-scalar archaeological and historical evidence concerning the eastern Caucasus beginning with the expansion of the Achaemenid Empire into this space and continuing through periods of intense Roman and Parthian interest in the space. The vectors of contact and exchange explored help us understand the shape of regional networks operating in the Caspian zone at different scales and within different social strata, and in doing so allow us to re-integrate the eastern Caucasus into broader patterns that crosscut the Iranian, Steppe, and Mediterranean worlds. But I moreover argue for the importance of the Caspian Sea as a corridor—an oft-overlooked north-south axis of connectivity—in the development of Eurasia in the second half of the first millennium BCE.

events.title: Student Faculty Macro Lunch: "House Prices and Quantities Around the World"
events.description: Abstract: We establish several first-order facts using house price and quantity data for middle- and high-income countries. First, housing units and rooms per person rise with per capita income and then asymptote so that additional increases in income are uncorrelated with housing quantities. Second, growth in housing units is strongly correlated with population growth at all income levels. Third, real house prices and housing expenditure shares rise in near-constant proportion with per capita income. A model with non-homothetic demand for home space, homothetic demand for housing quality, and upward-sloping supply of the unit-quality housing bundle can explain these relationships. A standard model where unit-supply is increasingly inelastic does not match the facts.

events.title: Black Critical Theory Initiative: Cecilio M. Cooper
events.location: 820 Social Sciences Building, the Social Sciences Matrix
events.description: "'Seeing Hints of a Trans Fella': Holotypic Black Feminisms, Stereoscopic Transantagonisms" Impelled by Hortense Spillers' and Sylvia Wynter's interventions, the 'black female', 'black woman', 'black femme', 'black feminine,' 'black girl', 'black mother', 'bulldagger', and so on have become valorized topics of gender analysis while also being intermittently leveraged to camouflage collusion with negrophobic antitrans retrenchment. Suffering deemed intrinsic to both structural emplotment beneath these specific racial headings and the sex-gender binary writ large has long been narrated as stemming from black experiences with coercive masculinization. This talk not only critically appraises black transmasculinity's aporetic function for cis-aspirant parsings of black female/woman from black male/man. Via psychosexual questions about aesthetics, taxonomy, and visuality, it likewise contends with the ways black transmasculinity and black trans manhood have been deployed as foils to ideal trans(gender) subjectivity.Cecilio M. Cooper's first monograph examines the occulted roles blackness and darkness play throughout the visual cultures of alchemy and demonology while the second contends with depictions of black transmasculinity across art and media. They have held postdoctoral fellowships in History of Science at the Science History Institute's Beckman Center for the History of Chemistry and in History of Art at the University of Michigan-Ann Arbor. Their research has also been previously supported by Long-Term fellowships from the Folger Shakespeare Library, National Endowment for the Humanities, and American Antiquarian Society. Alongside their scholarship and criticism, Cooper's creative practice draws from performance, moving image, and sculpture. They completed a PhD with distinction in Black Studies and a Graduate Certificate in Critical Theory from Northwestern University as well as an MA in Performance Studies with a Designated Emphasis in Feminist Theory & Research from the University of California-Davis.

events.title: A Book is Born: The Pleasure of Texting
events.description: Lynne Huffer (Emory) and Mario Telò (Berkeley) had long admired one another's work, but always at a distance. The two met in person for the first time in fall 2025, when Huffer visited the Bay Area. A Saturday trip to the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art sparked the first of what would become thousands of texting exchanges, ranging from reflections on the banalities of daily life to sustained philosophical conversations. This text chain eventually became the basis for their coauthored book, The Pleasure of Texting: Sapphic Writing and Reading at the Edge of the World, forthcoming from Duke University Press.The Pleasure of Texting explores what it means to think across different intellectual, academic, and personal experiences. The authors' collaboration takes the form of a poetic riffing in which intellectual difference becomes generative. The rhythms of digital communication — with its waiting, gaps, and moments of connection — become part of the writing itself. The result is not a fusion of two voices but a juxtapositional form in which the authors play off of one another. In conversation with their editor, Ryan Kendall (Duke UP), Huffer and Telò explore the capacity of texting as a new model of collaborative writing, in which quotidian, obsessive texting is shaped into paragraphs, chapters, and eventually a book.

events.title: Ariel Tang | Scripting Silence: Animals Political and Unpolitical in Charlotte Beradt's Dreamscape
events.description: This talk features the implicit dialogue between the German-Jewish journalist Charlotte Beradt (1907-1986) and her fellow émigré, Hannah Arendt, regarding the boundaries between humans and animals, as well as the ethical limits of anthropocentrism during political crises. Beradt's Third Reich of Dreams, a catalogue of dreams compiled between 1933 and 1939 on the basis of dreams retold by more than fifty Germans living under totalitarian rule, prompts her readers to re-evaluate the unique traits of physiological activities such as dreaming—as opposed to discursive reasoning—in safeguarding the humane promise of politics. While conventional pictures of human nature often fall prey to naturalistic or essentialist tendencies, the vital dialogue between Beradt and Arendt helps to resuscitate the unmistakable normative value of anthropological evidence, the substance of which often escapes the immediate capture of language and yet preserves the hope for political renewal lost in effable experience. Ariel Tang is a Postdoctoral Fellow in the Department of Political Science at Stanford University. Her research focuses on Enlightenment political thought and its legacies, with special attention to questions related to knowledge institutions, education, and the interactions between culture and nature. Her current book manuscript traces an entangled history of the idea of Bildung and the rise of the modern research university. She received her bachelor's degree in Philosophy from Barnard College, Columbia University, and her PhD in Political Science from Yale University. events.title: PMB Seminar with Lila Fishman | The genomics of multi-trait adaptation to Yellowstone's geothermal soil mosaic in monkeyflowers
events.description: Environmental mosaics can generate strong divergent selection on plant traits even in the face of cross- habitat gene flow, leading to microgeographic local adaptation and (perhaps) incipient speciation. Here, we use yellow monkeyflower adaptation to the fine-scaled yet physically-extreme mosaic of soil conditions in the geyser basins of Yellowstone National Park to explore fundamental questions about the genomic and molecular mechanisms of adaptation to extreme conditions. For two traits with simple genetic bases (trichome density and minimum critical photoperiod for flowering), candidate variants in predictable molecular pathways underlie dramatic phenotypic divergence over a 100m scale gradient. In contrast, a novel multi-gene locus (out6 supergene) co-ordinates plant architecture and phenological traits underlying a unique-to-Yellowstone thermal annual strategy. The out6 locus draws on both old (but novel relative to known life-history polymorphisms) standing variation and recent introgression to confer adaptation to extreme thermal soils, and contains several strong functional candidates. Finally, although Yellowstone thermal annuals are highly specialized to the unique niche created by winter snowmelt on hot soils, thus escaping summer's deadly heat and drought, they have also evolved remarkable xylem drought/heat resistance. Together, these instances of extreme local adaptation provide a composite picture of how different plant traits and pathways evolve in response to novel environments.

events.title: Sappho and Critical Theory
events.description: Taking inspiration from the Sapphic collages of Lynne Huffer on display at the Townsend Center through May 2027, this symposium gathers together scholars working at the intersection of philosophy, literature, and creative practice. Speakers reflect on the ways in which Sappho and the Sapphic tradition have contributed in subterranean ways to counterintuitive modes of thinking — and thus to the radical work of critical theory, broadly defined. Because so little of her work survives intact, Sappho has long been particularly available for reinterpretation. Engaging with this rich field of possibility, panelists ask: can we see Sappho as a philosopher or critical theorist who preemptively contests the all-male tradition that brackets her in the domain of ancient poetry? Can we approach her oeuvre as a practice of feminist and transfeminist production that problematizes the very distinction between poetry and philosophy? How does an approach that emphasizes the discontinuous and fragmentary state of the archive change our perceptions of Sappho — such as her traditional association with Victorian and post-Victorian models of white lesbianism? How can a fresh return to Sappho help us navigate a moment in which gender is increasingly entangled with fear, anxiety, and political contestation? Following the symposium, audience members are invited to the Townsend Center for a reception to celebrate the opening of the exhibition, Thinking with Sappho: Lynne Huffer and the Art of Collage. events.description: This project examines the international dimensions of Black radicalism and the prospects and complications of multilateral solidarity in the 21st century. 2025 and 2026 have seen the acceleration of draconian immigration policies and the reinforced legitimacy and expansion of police and prison institutions in the U.S. These developments have demonstrated how the carceral state and western imperialism operate as collaborative forces. The fates of racialized communities in the U.S. and oppressed communities throughout the Global South are therefore deeply interconnected. This project engages participant-observer methods that involve delegations of Los Angeles youth activists in immersive traveling experiences to critical locations of Black radical developments. These delegations endeavored to connect and build community with local activists, artists, and farmers and to engage the Black radical tradition as a precondition for effective and meaningful solidarity in advancing movements for sovereignty, self-determination, reparations, and economic justice. These locations include Cuba, Puerto Rico, and South Africa.Gabriel is the UC Chancellor's Postdoctoral Fellow in the Department of African American and African Studies at UC Davis and he studies Pan Africanism, the Black radical tradition, Marxist theory, abolition theory, and Caribbean and African decolonization. He earned his Ph.D. in African Diaspora Studies and Critical Theory at UC Berkeley.

events.title: CLIMB + Neyman Seminar with Susan Murphy: Online Reinforcement Learning for Digital Health Interventions in the Dyadic Setting
events.description: Please join us for a joint CLIMB + Neyman Seminar with Susan Murphy Online Reinforcement Learning for Digital Health Interventions in the Dyadic Setting Abstract We present our ongoing work on the development of an online reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm that personalizes delivery of interventions sequentially, over time, to members of a dyad. The RL algorithm is one component in the design of the digital health intervention. Different RL components target different elements of the dyad; these elements are a target individual, a carepartner and their relationship. The RL algorithm is a multi-agent RL algorithm in which the 3 agents make decisions on the 3 elements of the dyad. We incorporate domain knowledge in the form of approximal causal directed acyclic graphs to speed up online learning in this sparse data setting. This work is motivated by our development of the ADAPTS-HCT multi-agent RL algorithm, designed to improve medication adherence by young adults who have undergone a blood and bone marrow transplant. The RL algorithm will be deployed in a clinical trial in late summer 2026. BioSusan A. Murphy is Mallinckrodt Professor of Statistics and of Computer Science and Associate Faculty at the Kempner Institute, Harvard University. Her research focuses on improving sequential decision making via the development of online, real-time reinforcement learning algorithms. Her lab is involved in multiple deployments of these algorithms in digital health. She is a member of the US National Academy of Sciences and of the US National Academy of Medicine. In 2013 she was awarded a MacArthur Fellowship for her work on experimental designs to inform sequential decision making. She is a Fellow of the College on Problems in Drug Dependence, Past-President of Institute of Mathematical Statistics, Past-President of the Bernoulli Society and a former editor of the Annals of Statistics. CLIMB Voleon Seminars are organized by the Center for the Theoretical Foundations of Learning, Inference, Information, Intelligence, Mathematics, and Microeconomics at Berkeley (CLIMB), and are generously supported by the Voleon Group. CLIMB addresses new conceptual and mathematical challenges arising at the interface between technology, science, and society.If you require an accommodation for effective communication or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact Naomi Yamasaki at climb-support@eecs.berkeley.edu (mailto:naomiy@berkeley.edu) or 510-710-8488 with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days before the event.

events.title: MBN Seminar: Identification of Novel Targets to Reverse Hepatic Fibrogenesis
events.description: Dr. Jennifer Y. Chen, Associate Professor, Department of Medicine, Division of Gastroenterology and Hepatology, UC San Francisco Dr. Jennifer Y. Chen is a physician-scientist and hepatologist at the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF). She completed her medical training at Harvard, where she also pursued postdoctoral research in hepatic stellate cell biology and the molecular mechanisms of liver fibrogenesis. Her research program integrates basic, translational, and clinical investigation to advance precision medicine for patients with chronic liver disease. Focusing on the cellular and molecular pathways that drive hepatic fibrosis, her laboratory is developing novel antifibrotic therapies through collaborations with medicinal chemists to design and optimize small-molecule inhibitors that target key fibrogenic pathways. In parallel, her team is discovering and validating biomarkers that improve the diagnosis, risk stratification, and therapeutic monitoring of patients with liver fibrosis. Her work aims to accelerate the translation of mechanistic discoveries into innovative, personalized treatments that improve outcomes for patients with chronic liver disease.

events.title: Living Literature: Roland Barthes, Citation, and the Reading of Everyday Life | A Talk with Professor John Lurz (Tufts)
events.description: Please join the UC Berkeley Department of English at 5 pm in Wheeler Hall, Room 300, for "Living Literature: Roland Barthes, Citation, and the Reading of Everyday Life," a talk with Professor John Lurz (Tufts). John Lurz's lecture, drawn from his recent book The Barthes Fantastic: Literature, Criticism, and the Practice of Language (Chicago, 2025), revisits the writings of Roland Barthes to examine citation as an intellectual practice that mobilizes fragments of particular texts to galvanize our conventional or mythologized sense of the world. Enlarging our sense of what we learn as students of literature, Lurz introduces a new conceptual category or way of thinking that he calls "the fantastic," in which the texts we read come to inform the texture of our lives.

events.title: Film Screening: It Will Be Better Before and Temo Re
events.description: It Will Be Better Before began as a collaboration between two directors. After five years, one of the directors, Keto Kipiani, re-edited and modified the film, sharing her perspective and feelings throughout the creation process. "The title, with its mixed tenses that collapse time, conveys the confused desperation of a future torn from one's control … a personal story about hanging onto glimmers of meaning but also, implicitly and inevitably, a national one" (Carmen Gray, Senses of Cinema). With Temo Re, photographer and filmmaker Anka Gujabidze creates a multifaceted portrait of Georgia's capital city, Tbilisi. The protagonist, an actor who earns his living as a motorcycle courier, is played by Temo Rekhviashvili, the author of Courier's Tales, the novel upon which the film is based. Composed of thousands of black-and-white still images, this unique film won the Best Short Film Award when it premiered at the International Film Festival Rotterdam.

events.title: Maayan Levy: Toward the development of metabotherapy
events.description: Diet can be a powerful, low-cost lever for treating disease. We previously showed that a ketogenic diet suppresses intestinal tumorigenesis in mouse models of colorectal cancer, mediated by the metabolite beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB) acting through HCAR2 to induce the differentiation factor HOPX (Dmitrieva-Posocco et al., Nature, 2022). A follow-up trial in Lynch syndrome patients confirmed that BHB supplementation reduces colonic epithelial proliferation, and a clinical trial for colorectal cancer prevention is now underway (NCT05338307). We asked whether the same metabolite could address a different problem: CAR T cell therapy fails in roughly half of patients and rarely works in solid tumors. Screening diets in mouse lymphoma models, we found that a ketogenic diet- again acting through BHB- potentiates CAR T cell function, fueling the TCA cycle and reprogramming T cells away from exhaustion toward a more cytotoxic state. BHB supplementation alone dramatically improved tumor clearance and survival in lymphoma and solid tumor models, and enhanced T cell metabolic fitness in healthy human volunteers, motivating an ongoing Phase I trial combining BHB with CAR T cell therapy in lymphoma patients. Together, this work suggests that a single, inexpensive dietary metabolite can be repurposed across cancer prevention and immunotherapy to meaningfully improve patient outcomes.Division(s): MTx (Molecular Therapeutics)

events.title: Lecture | Taking God Seriously in Modern Islamic Politics: Muhammad al-Ghazali (1917–1996), Science, and Divine Presence in Twentieth-Century Egypt
events.description: Abstract: In his new book, Mediating God: Muhammad al-Ghazali and the Politics of Divine Presence in Twentieth-Century Egypt, Arthur Zárate argues that although God stands at the center of contemporary Muslim moral and political visions, the deity's presence is often neglected in scholarship. This talk explores why that neglect persists and what comes into focus when theological claims are taken seriously in the study of modern Islamic politics. Focusing on the Egyptian theologian Muhammad al-Ghazali (1917–1996), it examines his engagements with modern scientific discourses to show how science became one avenue through which divine presence was encountered and affirmed. Debates over science, it argues, were simultaneously debates about God, and competing understandings of the natural world underwrote competing visions of political and social reform. Ultimately, the talk proposes "activist theology" as a more adequate framework than "Islamism" for understanding al-Ghazali's politics.Bio: Arthur Zárate is a historian of the modern Middle East whose research explores the intersections of politics, science, and theology in modern Islam. He is the author of Mediating God: Muhammad al-Ghazali and the Politics of Divine Presence in Twentieth-Century Egypt (Oxford University Press, 2025). His work has appeared in Comparative Studies in Society and History and the Journal of the American Academy of Religion, and is forthcoming in the International Journal of Middle East Studies. He is Assistant Professor of Global Humanities at San José State University, where he teaches in the Honors Humanities Program. He is currently writing a second book on Sufism, spiritual experimentation, and Muslim and Coptic saintly mediation in modern Egypt.

events.title: Life ascending: mechanisms of environmental adaptation in extreme high-elevation Andean mice
events.description: A fundamental goal in evolutionary biology is to understand how the realized niche of a given species has been shaped by local adaptation to extreme environmental conditions, such as those that prevail at range margins. Investigation of local adaptation of montane species at their upper elevational range limits may be especially informative in this effort. Andean leaf-eared mice, Phyllotis vaccarum, live on the summits of 6700 m volcanoes in the Puna de Atacama, far surpassing the known elevational range limits of all other terrestrial vertebrates. Such elevations were previously thought to be uninhabitable by mammals due to severe hypoxia and frigid temperatures. In addition to holding the record as the highest-dwelling mammal, P. vaccarum also has the broadest elevational range, as it is distributed from sea level along the desert coast of northern Chile up to the crest of the Andean Cordillera. Here I report results of physiological and genomic analyses that provided new insights into mechanisms of physiological adaptation to extreme elevations in P. vaccarum. Our genomic analysis also revealed unanticipated dimensions of environmental adaptation related to feeding ecology.

events.title: Two Provinces, Two Paths: Canada and the Independence Debate in Alberta and Quebec
events.description: This panel will discuss the recent rise of sovereigntist and independentist politics in Quebec and Alberta. The pro-independence arguments in each province advance different motivations rooted in unique regional histories. However, they also share a sense of alienation from "Canadian" culture and national identity. What factors are causing this resurgence of sovereignist feeling in Canada? How are proponents of Canadian federalism responding to their grievances? And how are international developments, including heightened Canada-US tensions, shaping the trajectory of these movements?About the PanelistsMartha Hall Findlay is the Director and Palmer Chair in Public Policy, School of Public Policy, University of Calgary; a member of the Expert Group on Canada-U.S. Relations. A former two-term Member of Parliament, she served on the Official Opposition shadow cabinet as well as on committees concerned with trade, finance, and public works. Before politics, she worked as an international corporate lawyer and senior executive for Suncor Energy and the Canada West Foundation. She is currently overseeing the official Alberta government report on the economic impact to the province of leaving Canada.Philippe Gervais is a seasoned leader in communications and public affairs with more than 30 years of experience across the public and private sectors. He currently serves as the Vice-President, Communications and Institutional Relations, for McGill University. Before joining McGill, Mr. Gervais was a Managing Principal for Navigator Ltd, a Canadian crisis management, government relations and public opinion company. He has worked for both the Federal and Quebec provincial governments, and he has advised political campaigns at all levels of government across Canada.Kristina Michaud was elected to Canada's House of Commons at age 26, becoming one of the youngest federal representatives ever elected. From 2019 to 2025, she served as a Bloc Québécois MP and as the party's critic for Public Safety and Climate Change. Originally from eastern Quebec, she now works as a political analyst and commentator for various television and radio programs and writes in La Presse.Martin Pelletier, CFA is a senior portfolio manager, investment fund manager, author, and financial columnist. He is a recognized market strategist, regularly contributing to Canada's Financial Post and appearing in Canadian and US media to provide insights on topics including equity and bond markets, monetary and fiscal policy, and oil and gas and commodities. events.title: Arash Afraz - How Does the Activity of Visually Responsive Neurons Generate Visual Perception?
events.description: We typically study the mechanistic underpinnings of vision by observing how "visually responsive" neurons in the brain respond to and encode visual stimuli. While highly informative, this approach is indirect and correlational and does not reveal the causal contribution of these neurons to visual perception. In this talk, I will introduce a new methodology, Perceptography, that quantitatively and graphically determines the causal role of cortical neurons in perception. I will then propose a new roadmap and theoretical framework for understanding visual perception.

events.title: Ned Wingreen: Collective dynamics in B cell affinity maturation
events.description: In the humoral immune response, B cells that produce high-affinity antibodies are generated through a Darwinian evolutionary process called affinity maturation. Affinity maturation, which takes place in germinal centers (GC), is driven by cycles of selection (mediated by T cells), division, and hypermutation of B cells. Recently, it was found that the T cells themselves also exhibit dynamic behavior throughout the course of the GC reaction, undergoing affinity-dependent proliferation. A model suggests that this reciprocal stimulation enforces a robust "homeostatic" regulation of the relative number of B cells and T cells in the GC, leading to a constant ratio of GC lymphocytes. But the model also points to a problem: the high mutation rate of GC B cells can lead to "backsliding" of affinity. The proposed solution – a fitness-dependent mutation rate – has been experimentally verified, and has implications beyond B cell affinity maturation.Division(s): INFORMAL SEMINAR

Talk Summary: Drawing on insights from the co-authored book The Korean Startup Ecosystem: Past, Present, and Future, this lecture offers an insider's perspective on Korea's evolving innovation landscape. It traces the nation's transition from a conglomerate-driven growth model to an innovation-led economy, highlighting the critical interplay between venture capital, government policy, conglomerates, and entrepreneurial culture. The talk demonstrates how Korea's global cultural powerhouses—including K-pop, K-dramas, and K-beauty—are strategic outcomes of this systematically built ecosystem. Through a comparative lens, the lecture examines the institutional features that distinguish the Korean and U.S. markets across key dimensions like financing, risk tolerance, and policy intervention. It concludes by outlining strategic implications for global founders, investors, and policymakers, followed by an interactive Q&A session. The English edition of The Korean Startup Ecosystem: Past, Present, and Future is available for download for free at the following link for those who are interested: https://bit.ly/4tNQSAJ (https://bit.ly/4tNQSAJ) Speaker Bio: Professor Paik is a tenured professor at the KAIST College of Business and an affiliated professor at the KAIST College of AI. His research explores the intersection of entrepreneurship, innovation, strategy, institutions, and public policy. He serves as an editorial review board member and referee for numerous top-tier academic journals in his field, and his research has appeared in premier publications such as the Strategic Management Journal, Organization Science, Strategic Entrepreneurship Journal, and the Journal of Economics & Management Strategy. Before joining KAIST in 2018, Professor Paik served as an assistant professor at the University of Southern California's Marshall School of Business and Washington University in St. Louis's Olin Business School. He holds a Ph.D. in Economics from the University of California, Berkeley. Prior to his academic career, he was a patent attorney at the leading South Korean law firm Kim & Chang, advising both multinational corporations and entrepreneurial ventures. A seasoned advisor in the innovation ecosystem, Professor Paik cofounded the venture capital firm TBW Investment, which was later acquired via M&A.
